title: The family tree of life: how scientists work out who is related to whom, and how long ago their lines split

summary.text: A dolphin looks like a shark, yet the dolphin's closest relatives are hippos and cows. How can anyone know that, when nobody was there to watch the family lines split? In this lesson you build trees from bodies and from DNA, and you choose between trees by counting changes. Then you roll a die to find out whether chance copying mistakes can tell time. You use your own dice clock to date a split that a grown-up keeps secret.
summary.art: A dolphin, a shark and a cow drawn in a row, with a forked line joining the dolphin and the cow first, and a die and a strip of thirty squares below them.

intro.hook: A hippo stands in an African river. A blue whale swims in the open sea. Scientists say these two are closer relatives than a hippo and a pig. Nobody saw their family lines split. So how do scientists know, and how do they know when it happened?
intro.text: Nobody has a birth record for a whale. What we have are bodies, fossils and DNA. DNA is the long molecule that carries the instructions for building a body, written in four chemical letters. The cells of every living being hold DNA. In this lesson you first guess who is whose cousin from looks alone, and keep your guesses. You count the changes that three different trees would need, and pick the tree that needs the fewest. You roll a die seventy times to see whether chance mistakes add up steadily enough to work as a clock. Then you follow the case of the whale, where teeth, DNA and ankle bones each pointed somewhere. You also meet a purple frog from Kerala whose nearest relatives live on islands far across the Indian Ocean.
intro.art: A child at a table rolling a die beside a steel tumbler of numbered paper chits and a paper strip with some squares coloured in.

outcomes: By the end I can read a family tree by its forks, and say who is whose closer relative.
By the end I can explain why shared new features show family, and why lookalike features can mislead.
By the end I can choose between possible trees by counting which needs the fewest changes.
By the end I can explain how chance copying mistakes can keep time, using my results from the Dice Clock Test.
By the end I can say how a molecular clock is set with a fossil, and why its answer comes with a range.
By the end I can give three surprising pairs of cousins, and the evidence for each.
By the end I can explain why fast genes and slow genes suit different questions, and why two genes can give two trees.

terms.meaning: A phylogeny is the family history of a group of living beings. It shows which family lines split from which, and in what order.
terms.example: The phylogeny of the big cats shows that lions and leopards share a more recent ancestor than lions and house cats do.
terms.art: A small branching diagram with a lion, a leopard and a house cat at the three tips.

terms.meaning: A common ancestor is a parent population that two or more living groups both descend from.
terms.example: You and your cousin have a common ancestor in your grandmother. A crow and a crocodile have a common ancestor who lived about 243 million years ago.
terms.art: Two children with lines going up to one grandmother, beside a crow and a crocodile with lines going up to one small reptile.

terms.meaning: A fork is the point on a family tree where one line splits into two. Each fork stands for a common ancestor. Scientists also call a fork a node.
terms.example: On a tree of apes, the fork that joins the human line and the chimpanzee line is about 6.5 million years old.
terms.art: A Y-shaped fork drawn large, with a dot at the join and an arrow pointing to the dot.

terms.meaning: Sister groups are the two branches that come out of one fork. Each is the other's closest relative.
terms.example: Whales and hippos are sister groups. Crocodiles and birds are sister groups.
terms.art: A fork with a whale on one tip and a hippo on the other.

terms.meaning: A clade is one ancestor together with all of the descendants. You can cut a clade off a tree with a single snip.
terms.example: Birds are a clade. 'Animals that fly' is no clade, because bats, birds and butterflies got their wings separately.
terms.art: A tree with scissors cutting one branch, and all the twigs on that branch falling away together.

terms.meaning: A shared new feature is a feature that first appeared in one ancestor and was passed to all the descendants. Scientists call this a shared derived feature.
terms.example: Milk is a shared new feature of mammals. A dolphin mother and a cow mother both feed milk, because both inherited it from the first mammals.
terms.art: A dolphin calf drinking from the mother and a calf drinking from a cow, with a line joining both to one small furry ancestor.

terms.meaning: A lookalike feature is a feature that two groups evolved separately, because they live in the same way. Scientists call this convergent evolution.
terms.example: A shark and a dolphin both have a smooth shape and fins. The shark's tail fin stands upright. The dolphin's tail fin lies flat.
terms.art: A shark and a dolphin side by side, with the shark's upright tail fin and the dolphin's flat tail fin circled.

terms.meaning: An outsider is a living being known to be a more distant relative than all the others on your tree. Comparing with the outsider shows which features are old and which are new. Scientists call this an outgroup.
terms.example: To build a tree of a shark, a dolphin and a cow, you can use an earthworm as the outsider.
terms.art: A small tree of a shark, a dolphin and a cow, with an earthworm on a long branch standing apart at one side.

terms.meaning: When several trees are possible, scientists first try the tree that needs the fewest changes. A change is a feature appearing or being lost. The proper name is parsimony.
terms.example: If dolphins were sisters of sharks, then lungs, milk and hair would each have to appear twice. If dolphins are sisters of cows, each appears once.
terms.art: Two small trees side by side with tick marks on the branches, one tree with many marks and one with few.

terms.meaning: A DNA sequence is the order of the four chemical letters, A, C, G and T, along a piece of DNA.
terms.example: The first letters of one human gene read ATGGTGCAC. The same gene in a chimpanzee starts with the same letters.
terms.art: A strip of paper with the letters ATGGTGCAC written in boxes.

terms.meaning: A mutation is a change in a DNA sequence. Most mutations are copying mistakes made when a cell copies DNA.
terms.example: A cell copies three billion letters and gets a few of them wrong. Most of those changes make no difference to the body.
terms.art: Two rows of the same letters, one above the other, with a single letter different and circled.

terms.meaning: A molecular clock is a way of telling how long ago two family lines split. It counts the DNA differences between them, and uses the average rate at which mutations pile up.
terms.example: Human and chimpanzee DNA differ in about 1.2 letters in every 100. The clock puts the split at about 6.5 million years ago.
terms.art: A clock face whose numbers are replaced by the letters A, C, G and T, with a human and a chimpanzee on either side.

terms.meaning: A rate says how much of something happens in a set time.
terms.example: If 6 squares change in 20 rounds, the rate is 6 divided by 20, which is 0.3 squares in each round.
terms.art: A notebook sum reading '6 changes ÷ 20 rounds = 0.3 changes in each round'.

terms.meaning: Calibration means setting a measuring tool against something already known. A molecular clock is calibrated with a split whose date is known from fossils or rocks.
terms.example: A shopkeeper checks a weighing scale with a one-kilogram weight. A scientist checks a DNA clock with a dated fossil.
terms.art: A weighing scale with a one-kilogram weight on the pan, beside a fossil with a date label.

terms.meaning: A time tree is a family tree drawn to scale, so the place of each fork shows how long ago that split happened.
terms.example: On a time tree where 1 centimetre is 10 million years, the fork between humans and rats is 8.4 centimetres back from today.
terms.art: A tree drawn sideways along a ruler, with forks at different distances from the right-hand edge marked 'today'.

terms.meaning: A hidden change is a second mutation at a place that has already changed. It cannot be seen by comparing two sequences, so very old splits can look younger than they are. Scientists call this problem saturation.
terms.example: In the Dice Clock Test, a square that is hit twice is still only one coloured square.
terms.art: A strip of squares with one coloured square that has a small dot inside.

terms.meaning: A bracket tree is a family tree written in one line. Each pair of brackets holds one fork, with the two sister branches inside.
terms.example: ((crow, crocodile), lizard) means the crow and the crocodile are sisters, and the lizard is the next closest relative of both.
terms.art: The words '((crow, crocodile), lizard)' written above the same tree drawn as forked lines.

explanations.concept: A family tree is read by its forks
explanations.definition: A family tree of life, or phylogeny, is a diagram of which family lines split from which. Each fork is a common ancestor, and each tip is a group living today or a fossil group.
explanations.description: Start with your own family. You and your sister share parents. You and your cousin share grandparents. Your sister is the closer relative, because the ancestors you share with her lived more recently. A tree of life works in the same way. To find how closely two tips are related, trace back from each until the lines meet. The more recent that fork, the closer the two are. The order of the tips along the top means nothing. Any fork can be turned round like a mobile on a thread, and the tree stays the same tree. Three mistakes are common. The first is to read the tips from left to right as a ladder from 'simple' to 'advanced'. Every living tip has been evolving for exactly the same length of time. The second is to think one living tip is the ancestor of another. Humans did not come from chimpanzees. Both came from an ancestor who was neither, and who lived about 6.5 million years ago. The third is to judge by how near two tips are drawn.
examples: On a tree of apes, the gorilla sits beside the chimpanzee in many drawings. Yet a gorilla is exactly as closely related to you as to a chimpanzee. The gorilla line split off before the human and chimpanzee lines parted.
((crow, crocodile), lizard) and (lizard, (crocodile, crow)) are the same tree. In both, the crow and the crocodile share a fork that the lizard is outside.
A rohu fish alive today is no more 'ancient' than you are. Your line and the rohu's line parted about 435 million years ago, and both have changed ever since.
explanations.art: The same tree of four animals drawn twice, with one fork flipped in the second drawing and an equals sign between the two.

explanations.concept: Building a tree from bodies: look for shared new features
explanations.definition: A shared new feature is one that appeared in a single ancestor and was passed on. Groups that share new features are placed together on the tree.
explanations.description: Not every likeness helps. A dolphin, a cow and a shark all have a backbone. That does not tell you which two are closer, because the backbone is old. All three inherited it from an ancestor far back. What helps is a feature that is newer than the group as a whole, and that only some members have. A dolphin and a cow both have lungs, milk, hair at some time in life and three tiny bones in each middle ear. A shark has none of these. So the dolphin and the cow share an ancestor that the shark's line had already left. The German insect scientist Willi Hennig set out this rule in a book in 1950. It was little noticed until an English version came out in 1966. Why does the rule work? A new feature appears once, in one population. Everyone descended from that population can inherit it. So a shared new feature is a mark left by one particular ancestor. Lookalike features are the trap. A way of life can shape unrelated bodies alike, and then the likeness says how they live, not who their parents were.
examples: Feathers are a shared new feature of birds and of some fossil dinosaurs. That is one reason scientists place birds inside the dinosaur branch.

A flying fox and a crow both have wings. Look inside and the wings differ. The bat's wing is skin stretched over long finger bones. The crow's wing is feathers on an arm with joined finger bones. The wings are lookalike features.
Dolphin calves are born with a few whiskers on the snout, which soon fall out. Even this small trace of hair marks the dolphin as a mammal.
explanations.art: A table with a shark, a dolphin and a cow down the side and features across the top, with ticks showing that the dolphin and the cow share lungs, milk and hair.

explanations.concept: Choosing between trees: count the changes
explanations.definition: Parsimony is the rule of trying first the tree that needs the fewest changes. A change is a feature appearing once or being lost once.
explanations.description: For three living groups and an outsider, three trees are possible. Any two of the three might be the sisters. Scientists test each tree against the features. Take one feature that two groups have. If those two are sisters on the tree, the feature needed to appear only once, in their shared ancestor. If they are not sisters, it needed two changes. Either it appeared twice, or it appeared once and was lost once. Add up the changes for every feature. The tree with the smallest total is the first choice. Why prefer fewer changes? A new feature such as milk needs many genes to change together over a long time. For that to happen twice in the same way is much less likely than once. The rule is a starting point and not a proof. When many features are lookalikes, the count can point to the wrong tree. So scientists use as many features as they can, and today most of the features are DNA letters.
examples: With eight features of a shark, a dolphin and a cow, the tree with the dolphin and the cow as sisters needs 10 changes. The tree with the dolphin and the shark as sisters needs 14.
With only the two features 'fish shape' and 'lives in the sea', the count would favour the dolphin and the shark. Two features are too few.
A computer can count changes on millions of possible trees. With 10 groups there are more than 34 million possible trees.
explanations.art: Three small trees of a shark, a dolphin and a cow, each with tick marks on the branches and a total written below: 14, 10 and 16.

explanations.definition: A DNA tree is built by lining up the same stretch of DNA from several living beings and comparing the letters, place by place.
explanations.description: DNA gives far more features than bodies do. A body offers some hundreds of features to compare. Two DNA sequences offer millions of places, and each place is a small feature of its own. Scientists first line the sequences up, so that each letter sits above the matching letter in the other species. Then a computer searches for the tree that explains the pattern best. Proteins were used before DNA could be read. In 1966 the American scientist Margaret Dayhoff, with Richard Eck, used a computer to build family trees from protein sequences. It was the first time anyone had done so. Some DNA features are especially trustworthy. One kind is a 'jumping gene'. This is a short piece of DNA that sometimes copies itself into a new place among the three billion letters. The chance of the same piece landing in exactly the same place twice is tiny. So if two species have the same jumping gene at the same place, they got it from one ancestor. Shared mistakes are strong evidence for the same reason. A correct letter could be correct in anyone. A rare mistake shared by two species is best explained by one ancestor who made it.
examples: In 1997 Mitsuru Shimamura, Norihiro Okada and their team in Japan found jumping genes at the same places in whales, hippos and cattle. Camels and pigs did not have them.
Humans, chimpanzees and gorillas all carry the same broken gene for making vitamin C. A shared broken gene is hard to explain without a shared ancestor.
During the COVID-19 years, scientists read the virus's sequence from patients all over the world. They drew its family tree week by week, and so could see where each new variant had come from.
explanations.art: Three rows of DNA letters lined up one above another, with a short coloured block inserted at the same place in two of the rows.

explanations.concept: The molecular clock: chance mistakes that keep time
explanations.definition: A molecular clock uses the number of DNA differences between two family lines to work out how long ago the lines split.
explanations.description: Each time DNA is copied, a few letters are copied wrongly. Nobody can say which letter will change next, or when. Each mistake is a chance event. But chance events in large numbers are steady. You cannot say which roll of a die will be a six. You can be nearly sure that 600 rolls will give close to 100 sixes. Most mutations fall in stretches of DNA where they make no difference to the body. Natural selection has nothing to act on there, so these changes simply pile up, at about the rate at which the mistakes are made. The Japanese scientist Motoo Kimura argued this in 1968. After two lines split, each line collects changes of their own. So the number of differences between them keeps growing, roughly in step with time. Count the differences, divide by the rate, and you have a time. Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling first proposed this in the 1960s. They had compared a blood protein, haemoglobin, across mammals. In 1965 they wrote that there may be 'a molecular evolutionary clock'.
examples: In the Dice Clock Test, a strip rolled for 40 rounds ends with about 11 coloured squares, and a strip rolled for 10 rounds ends with about 3. No single roll could have been predicted.
Human and chimpanzee DNA differ at about 1.2 places in every 100, in the parts that can be lined up. Human and macaque DNA differ at several times as many.
A new baby has some dozens of new mutations that neither parent had. One study of families in Iceland, published in 2012, counted them directly.
explanations.art: Two family lines drawn as two rows of squares running away from one starting square, each line gaining a few more coloured squares at every step.

explanations.concept: Setting the clock: a known date, and an honest range
explanations.definition: To calibrate a molecular clock is to work out its rate from a split whose date is already known.
explanations.description: Counting differences gives a number, such as 12 changes in every 1,000 letters. That is not yet a date. To turn it into years you need the rate, and the rate has to be measured against something known. Usually the known thing is a fossil. Suppose the oldest fossil that clearly belongs to one branch lies in rock 50 million years old. Then that branch had split off by 50 million years ago at the latest. The rock itself is dated from radioactive atoms. Sometimes the known thing is the Earth. When a piece of land breaks away and drifts off, the animals who cannot cross the sea are split at about that time. With one or more known dates, the scientist works out the rate. Then the same rate dates other splits that have no fossils. Every step has some error. The fossil gives only the latest possible date. The mistakes arrive by chance, so the count wobbles. So an honest clock date is always a range, such as '131 million years ago, and somewhere between 93 and 177'. Using many genes and many fossils narrows the range.
examples: In the Dice Clock Test you work out the rate from three strips whose rounds you know. Then you date a mystery strip. Three times out of four the answer lands within 10 rounds of the truth.
The website TimeTree gathers thousands of published clock studies. For the split between the human line and the hen's line it gives about 319 million years ago.

The purple frog of the Western Ghats and the tiny frogs of the Seychelles islands split about 131 million years ago, by the clock. India and the Seychelles broke apart about 65 million years ago. So the two frog families were already separate, and both rode the drifting land.
explanations.art: A time line with a fossil pinned at one known date, and a bracket around a second, undated fork showing a range of possible dates.

explanations.concept: Fast genes, slow genes and clocks that run at different speeds
explanations.definition: Different stretches of DNA change at different rates, and the rate can differ between kinds of living beings.
explanations.description: Some genes can hardly change at all, because nearly every change breaks something that every cell needs. These genes are slow. Other stretches of DNA can change freely, and they are fast. A fast stretch is good for recent splits, because it has had time to collect enough differences to count. Over a long time a fast stretch fills up. The same places get hit again and again, and the later hits are hidden changes. The count stops growing, so a very old split looks younger than it is. A slow gene is the opposite. It shows almost nothing for recent splits, and keeps counting steadily over hundreds of millions of years. So scientists choose the gene to suit the question. The rate also differs between family lines. Mice and rats collect changes faster each year than humans or elephants do. One likely reason is that their generations are short, so their DNA is copied more often each century. Modern methods let the rate vary from branch to branch. How far such 'relaxed' clocks can be trusted for the oldest splits is still argued about.
examples: In Fast Gene, Slow Gene, the fast strip tells 6 rounds from 12 rounds easily. The same strip is nearly full by 24 rounds, and can hardly tell 24 from 48.
The DNA in mitochondria changes fast in animals. It is used to compare populations of one species, and species that split recently.
The oldest clear fossils of animals are less than 600 million years old. Many molecular clocks put the first animals more than 100 million years earlier than that.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who build molecular clocks
perspectives.explanation: The first animals were small and soft and left almost no fossils. The clock sees a history that the rocks did not keep.
For the oldest splits, hidden changes and changing rates make the clock stretch. The true dates may be nearer to the first fossils.
Both are partly right. The clock gives a wide range for such old dates, and the range should be stated every time.

explanations.art: Two strips of twelve squares: one almost completely coloured in, and one with only three coloured squares.

explanations.definition: A surprising cousin is a close relative who looks or lives very differently, and whose kinship was found from DNA, fossils or both.
explanations.description: Bodies change fast when a way of life changes. So some of the closest relatives look nothing alike, and some lookalikes are far apart. Whales and dolphins are sisters of hippos. The dugong, the gentle sea cow of Palk Bay in Tamil Nadu, swims beside dolphins. Yet her nearer relatives are elephants and the small furry hyraxes of Africa. In 1998 DNA showed something larger. Elephants, sea cows, hyraxes, the aardvark, tenrecs, golden moles and elephant shrews form one old African branch of mammals, now called Afrotheria. No one had grouped them from their bodies alone. A mugger crocodile is a closer relative of a crow than of a garden lizard. Bats are closer to dogs and cows than to rats. In South India, the black Nilgiri langur was long grouped with the leaf monkeys of South-East Asia, whom they resemble. In 2008 Praveen Karanth, now at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru, and his co-workers compared DNA. They found that the Nilgiri langur's closest relatives are the grey Hanuman langurs living in the plains below.
examples: Hippo and whale: their lines split about 53 million years ago. The hippo's line and the pig's line split earlier, about 59 million years ago.
Dugong and elephant: about 61 million years ago. Dugong and dolphin: about 97 million years ago.
Crocodile and hen: about 243 million years ago. Garden lizard and hen: about 281 million years ago.
In your kitchen, the tomato's closest relative is the potato. Brinjal comes next and chilli after that. All four belong to one plant family.
explanations.art: Four pairs joined by forks: a whale with a hippo, a dugong with an elephant, a crocodile with a crow, and a tomato with a potato.

explanations.concept: When genes disagree with each other
explanations.definition: A gene tree is the family tree of one stretch of DNA. It usually matches the tree of the species, and sometimes does not.
explanations.description: Humans and chimpanzees are each other's closest living relatives, and gorillas come next. Yet in 2012, when the gorilla's DNA was read in full, scientists found something odd. In about 30 letters out of every 100, either the human or the chimpanzee sequence is closer to the gorilla's than to the other's. How can that be? The ancestor of all three was a large population, and that population held several versions of many stretches of DNA. The gorilla line split away first. Not long after, the human and chimpanzee lines parted. The time between the two splits was short. So by chance, the human line sometimes kept the same old version as the gorilla line, while the chimpanzee line kept another. For that stretch of DNA, the tree puts humans with gorillas. Nothing is wrong with either tree. A species tree is the tree that most of the DNA agrees on. This is why scientists no longer trust a tree built from one gene. They read thousands of stretches and report how many agree.
examples: Think of three sisters and their grandmother's bangles. The two younger sisters are closest in age, yet by chance the eldest and the youngest may have got the matching pair.
When splits come quickly one after another, as in the first birds after the dinosaurs died out, many gene trees disagree and the order of the splits is hard to settle.
When two splits are far apart in time, nearly every gene gives the same tree.
explanations.art: A wide tree of gorilla, chimpanzee and human drawn as a hollow tube, with a thin coloured line inside that joins the human and the gorilla first.

explanations.concept: Trees of anything that is copied
explanations.definition: Any set of things made by copying, with small mistakes passed on, has a family tree that can be rebuilt from the shared mistakes.
explanations.description: The method does not need DNA. It needs three things. Something is copied. The copies are sometimes wrong. A wrong copy passes the mistake on. Before printing, every book was copied by hand, and each copyist made slips. A copy made from a slipped copy carried the slip onward. Scholars of old books learned to group hand-written copies by their shared mistakes, long before anyone read DNA. In 1998 a team in Britain joined the two fields. They fed 58 hand-written copies of part of Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales into a computer program made for DNA. The program drew a family tree of the copies. Languages work in a similar way. Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada and Telugu share old words because they descend from one earlier language. So when you rebuild a family tree from DNA, you use a kind of reasoning that people have long used for books and words.
examples: Two recipe notebooks that both number two recipes '17' and none '18' were almost surely copied from one notebook with that slip.
Tamil 'kan', Malayalam 'kannu', Kannada 'kannu' and Telugu 'kannu' all mean eye. The likeness comes from one parent language.
A message passed along a line of whispering children changes a little at each child. The last versions on two branches of the line share the early changes.
explanations.art: Three hand-written notebooks open at the same page, with the same odd numbering circled in two of them.

explanations.concept: Two clocks made of chance: DNA and radioactive atoms
explanations.definition: A clock can be made from any change that happens by chance at a steady average rate. DNA mutations are one such change. The breakdown of radioactive atoms is another.
explanations.description: The fossil dates that set the molecular clock come from a second clock, inside rocks. Some kinds of atom are radioactive. This means the centre of the atom is unstable, and at some moment it breaks down and becomes a different kind of atom. Nobody can say when one such atom will break down. It may be in the next second or in a billion years. Yet in a lump of rock there are huge numbers of these atoms, and the fraction that breaks down each year is steady. Volcanic ash holds a radioactive kind of potassium. Half of it turns into other atoms in about 1.25 billion years. By measuring how much has turned, scientists date the ash, and so date the fossils lying between two ash layers. So the date of a split in the tree of life rests on two counts of chance events. One count is of changed letters in cells. The other is of changed atoms in stone. Why do the copying mistakes happen at all? The molecules that copy DNA are jostled all the time by heat. Ultraviolet light and natural radiation also damage letters now and then. A cell repairs nearly all of this, and a few changes slip through.
examples: The rocks in Kashmir that held the whale relative Indohyus are about 48 million years old.
The Deccan lava flows of Maharashtra are dated to about 66 million years ago by the radioactive clock.
A tossed coin is chance each time. A thousand tossed coins give very nearly 500 heads.
explanations.art: A layer of grey volcanic ash above and below a fossil bone in a cliff, with a small strip of coloured DNA squares drawn beside the bone.

explanations.concept: The frontier: the first fork of the animals, and the root of the whole tree
explanations.definition: The deepest forks of the tree of life are the hardest to place, and some are not settled.
explanations.description: The branches near the tips are well known. The deepest forks are harder, because so much time has passed and so many changes are hidden. One open case is the very first fork among the animals. For a long time most scientists thought sponges split off first. A sponge has no nerves and no muscles, so a sponge-like first animal seemed likely. From 2008 onward, some large DNA studies pointed instead to comb jellies. A comb jelly is a clear sea animal who swims with rows of tiny beating hairs, and who has nerves and muscles. In 2023 a team led by Darrin Schultz compared how genes are arranged along whole chromosomes. A chromosome is one long thread of DNA. They found that comb jellies still have an old arrangement that sponges and all other animals have lost. That points to comb jellies as the first to branch. If so, either nerves evolved twice, or sponges once had them and lost them. Many scientists accept the new result, and some still question it. At the very base of the tree, among bacteria and archaea, genes pass sideways between unrelated cells so often that some scientists draw a net there and not a tree.
examples: The same DNA data have given sponges first with one method of analysis and comb jellies first with another.
An arrangement of genes along a chromosome, once scrambled, almost never returns to the old order. That is why it is strong evidence.
For the split between the human line and the honeybee's line, the clock gives about 720 million years ago, with a range of about 650 to 800.

perspectives.who: Scientists who place comb jellies first
perspectives.explanation: The old arrangement of genes on comb jelly chromosomes is hard to explain in any other way. Bodies can become simpler, so the sponge's simple body proves little.
Comb jelly DNA has changed very fast, and fast-changing branches are easily misplaced by tree-building methods. The result should be repeated with more species.

explanations.art: A tree whose lowest fork is drawn twice in dotted lines, once with a sponge branching first and once with a comb jelly branching first, and a question mark between them.

agreed.text: All living beings on Earth are related, and their history has the shape of a branching tree for almost all animals, plants and fungi.
agreed.evidence: Every cell uses the same four DNA letters and nearly the same code for reading them. Trees built from bones, from proteins and from different genes agree with each other far more often than chance would allow.

agreed.text: How closely two living beings are related is decided by how recently their family lines split, not by how alike they look.
agreed.evidence: Sharks and dolphins look alike and split about 460 million years ago. Dolphins and cows look unlike and split about 57 million years ago. DNA, milk, lungs and ear bones all agree on this.

agreed.text: Whales descend from four-legged land mammals, and hippos are their closest living relatives.
agreed.evidence: DNA and jumping genes place whales beside hippos. In 2001 two teams found early whales with legs in Pakistan. Their ankle bones have the double-pulley shape of the hoofed group that includes hippos, cattle and deer.

agreed.text: DNA differences pile up roughly in step with time, so they can be used as a clock once the rate is set against known dates.
agreed.evidence: Clock dates set with one fossil have often been confirmed by fossils found later. The human and chimpanzee split of about 5 to 7 million years ago was first proposed from molecules in 1967, and later fossils fit it.

agreed.text: A clock date is a range, and the range is wider for older splits.
agreed.evidence: For the human and chimpanzee split, published studies give about 6.2 to 6.7 million years. For the human and honeybee split they give about 650 to 800 million years.

agreed.text: A tree built from one gene can differ from the tree of the species, so many genes are needed.
agreed.evidence: In the full gorilla DNA sequence published in 2012, about 30 letters in every 100 put the gorilla closer to humans or to chimpanzees than those two are to each other.

challenging.claim: Whales descend from mesonychids, a group of extinct meat-eating hoofed mammals.
challenging.who: Leigh Van Valen, an American scientist, from 1966, and most fossil experts until 2001
challenging.for: The teeth of the earliest fossil whales look very much like mesonychid teeth. For thirty years teeth were the best evidence anyone had.
challenging.against: DNA placed whales next to hippos. In 2001, ankle bones of early whales showed the double-pulley shape that hippos, cattle and deer have and mesonychids lack. The teeth were lookalike features.
challenging.context: This card is about an old answer to the question 'who are the whale's relatives?'. It was a good answer for its time, and new evidence showed it was wrong.

challenging.claim: The human line split from the other apes more than 15 million years ago.
challenging.who: Many fossil experts in the 1960s, including Elwyn Simons and, at first, David Pilbeam
challenging.for: Jaw pieces of a fossil ape called Ramapithecus, from the Siwalik Hills of India and Pakistan, seemed to have a human-like shape. They were many millions of years old.
challenging.against: In 1967 a protein clock gave about 5 million years. In 1982 a fossil face found in Pakistan showed that these apes were relatives of the orangutan.
challenging.context: This card is about when the human line parted from the line of the chimpanzees. Fossils and molecules first gave very different answers.

challenging.claim: The molecular clock ticks at one fixed rate in every living being and every gene.
challenging.who: An early, simple form of the clock idea in the 1960s
challenging.for: For one protein compared across similar animals, the number of differences does rise evenly with time.
challenging.against: Rates differ between genes, and between family lines. Rats and mice collect changes faster each year than humans do. Clocks today let the rate vary.
challenging.context: This card is about whether DNA changes pile up at the same speed everywhere. The simple version turned out to be too simple.

challenging.claim: Comb jellies, and not sponges, were the first animals to branch off from all the others.
challenging.who: Casey Dunn and others in 2008, and Darrin Schultz and others in 2023
challenging.for: Several large DNA studies, and the arrangement of genes on whole chromosomes, point to comb jellies.
challenging.against: Comb jelly DNA changes fast, which can mislead tree-building methods. Sponges have the simpler body, with no nerves or muscles.
challenging.context: This card is about the very first fork in the family tree of the animals. Scientists have not agreed on it.

challenging.claim: When DNA and bodies disagree, DNA is always right.
challenging.who: A common view among people who work only with DNA
challenging.for: DNA gives millions of features, and it settled the whale, the dugong and the langur cases.
challenging.against: Almost no fossil has DNA left, so the place of extinct groups rests on bones. DNA trees can also be wrong for fast-changing branches. The surest trees use both.
challenging.context: This card is about which evidence to trust when a tree from bones and a tree from DNA differ.

big_questions.q: In the Dice Clock Test, no roll could be predicted, yet the count told the time. How can chance events be steady?
big_questions.hint: Think about one roll and about seventy rolls. Which can you predict better, and why?

big_questions.q: A correct copy and a copy with a mistake: which one tells you more about where it came from?
big_questions.hint: Think of two classmates with the same right answer, and two with the same odd wrong answer.

big_questions.q: A dugong looks more like a dolphin than like an elephant. So what does 'closely related' really mean?
big_questions.hint: Think about your own cousins. Is the one who looks most like you always the closest relative?

big_questions.q: If you go back far enough, a banyan tree is your cousin. Does knowing that change how the tree looks to you?
big_questions.hint: There is no right answer. Notice what you feel when you look at a tree and say 'cousin'.

big_questions.q: Scientists were wrong about whales for thirty years, and then changed their minds. Is that a weakness of science or a strength?
big_questions.hint: Think about what made them change. Was it a louder voice, or something else?

big_questions.q: The date of a split is always given as a range. Would you trust a scientist more, or less, if she gave one exact number?
big_questions.hint: Think about your mystery strip. Was your answer exactly right?

story.title: Two Seventeens
story.note: Valli, her Aachi, the aunts, Dr Kamala Devi and the notebooks are made up. These things are real. Nattukottai Chettiar families of Karaikudi and the towns around it traded for generations in Burma, Malaya and Ceylon, and Chettiar families still live in Penang in Malaysia. Kavuni arisi is a Chettinad sweet made from black sticky rice, sugar or jaggery, ghee and coconut, and the rice is said to have first come home with traders from Burma. 'Aachi' is the Chettinad word for an elder woman or grandmother. Scholars really do work out the family tree of hand-copied books from the mistakes the copies share.
text: The letter from Penang came on a Tuesday, and Aachi read it standing up, which she never did.

"A Dr Kamala Devi," she said. "She teaches at a university in Malaysia. Her grandmother was called Unnamalai and came from a town in India beginning with K. She has found an old notebook of recipes in a trunk. She asks whether any family in Karaikudi knows the handwriting." Aachi folded the page. "There are a hundred towns beginning with K. And a thousand Unnamalais."

Valli was not really listening. She had her own trouble with notebooks. Aachi would be eighty in two weeks, and Valli had decided to make kavuni arisi for her, exactly as Aachi's own grandmother Meenakshi had made it. Meenakshi's recipe book had been eaten by white ants long ago. But her daughters had copied it by hand, and their daughters had copied the copies. Three copies were left. Valli had all three open on the swing in the hall.
They did not agree.
Aachi's copy said: cardamom, six pods. Periamma's copy, sent from Madurai, said sixty. So did Chitti's copy from Coimbatore.
"Sixty!" said Aachi. "You could clear a blocked nose from the next street."
"But two notebooks say sixty and only one says six," said Valli. "Two against one."

She did not like her own answer. That night she went through the copies page by page with a pencil. Periamma's copy spelt 'jaggery' with one g, every time. So did Chitti's. Periamma's copy had left out the brinjal pickle altogether. So had Chitti's. And Chitti's had a few slips of her own on top. In the pepper rasam, the pepper was missing.

Valli sat back. Chitti had not copied Meenakshi's book. She had copied Periamma's copy, mistakes and all, and added her own. Her 'sixty' was only Periamma's 'sixty' written out again. It was not two against one. It was one against one.
"So I still don't know," she told Aachi in the morning.
"You know more than you did," said Aachi. "Yesterday you were sure, and wrong."

Valli turned the pages of all three, looking for anything that would break the tie. That was when she noticed the numbers. In Aachi's copy the recipes were numbered down the margin. Fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, seventeen, nineteen. There were two seventeens, lime rice and tamarind rice, and no eighteen at all. She pulled Periamma's copy over. It had two seventeens. So did Chitti's.
"Aachi, did you know your notebook can't count?"

Aachi laughed. "That was my grandmother. She wrote the tamarind rice in late, between two others, and never fixed the numbers. My mother copied it just as it stood. She said it was not her place to correct her mother's book."
Valli looked at the two seventeens for a while. Then she looked at the letter on the shelf.
"Aachi. Write to the doctor in Penang. Ask her one thing. Ask her what number comes after seventeen."

The answer came in nine days, with photographs. Dr Kamala Devi wrote that she had never noticed until she was asked. In her grandmother's notebook, the lime rice was seventeen. The tamarind rice was seventeen. Then came nineteen.
Aachi sat down on the swing.

"Anyone can write 'six pods of cardamom'," said Valli. She was talking fast now. "That proves nothing. It is just correct. But nobody numbers two recipes seventeen by accident in the same place, in two countries. She has the mistake. So her notebook came from the same book as ours."
"Unnamalai," said Aachi slowly. "My grandmother had a younger daughter who sailed with her husband before the war. My mother spoke of a sister. Then letters stopped. I thought it was a story."

Valli was already bent over the photographs. The Penang notebook had none of Periamma's slips. Jaggery had two g's. The brinjal pickle was there. Unnamalai must have copied straight from her mother's book before she sailed. That made her copy a separate line from all three in India.
"Kavuni arisi," Valli read out. "Cardamom." She held her breath. "Six pods."
"Six," said Aachi. "I told you."

"You told me. But you could have been the one who was wrong. Now two lines that never met each other both say six." Valli read on down the page and stopped. "There is a line here that none of ours has. After the ghee. 'A pinch of salt, or the sweetness has no edge.'"
Aachi closed her eyes. "My mother must have skipped it," she said. "Sixty years I have been making it without the salt."
On the birthday, Valli soaked the black rice overnight and cooked it soft. She added six pods of cardamom, counted twice, and a pinch of salt. Aachi tasted it and said nothing for some time.
Then she asked for the telephone number in Penang.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the recipe copies are a family tree, and Valli rebuilds it the way scientists rebuild the tree of life. Two copies agreeing on 'sixty' looked like strong evidence. But one was copied from the other, so they counted as one voice. Shared mistakes showed that. The two seventeens are a mistake in the first book, so every true descendant carries it. That is how Valli knew the Penang notebook belonged to the family. A correct line could come from anywhere, and a rare shared mistake points to one source. Last, the Penang copy was a separate early branch. Where two separate branches agree, the reading most likely goes back to the first book. Scientists use shared rare changes in DNA in the same three ways.
ask: Two notebooks said sixty and one said six. Why was that not 'two against one'?
Why did the two seventeens prove more than a correctly copied line could?
Draw the family tree of the five notebooks: Meenakshi's, Aachi's, Periamma's, Chitti's and Unnamalai's.
The Penang notebook had a line about salt that the Indian copies lacked. On which branch of your tree was that line lost?
Where else could you rebuild a family tree from copies with mistakes?

games.title: Who Split First? The time line game
games.context: This is a card game about time trees. Each card names a living being. You place the card in a line, by how long ago you think their family line and the human line split. Then you turn the card over to check.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: One row for each player. Make a mark each time a card is placed wrongly. The fewest marks wins.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the names facing up. Do not look at the backs.
Take the top card and put it in the middle of the table, date side up. This starts the time line. Recent splits go on the left and older splits on the right.
On your turn, take the top card. Without turning it over, put it where you think it belongs in the line: at the left end, at the right end or between two cards.
Say your reason aloud. Then turn the card over.
If the date fits that place, the card stays. If not, move the card to the right place and take one mark.
Two cards with nearly the same date may go in either order.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the fewest marks wins.
Playing alone: try to place all 19 cards with 4 marks or fewer.

flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mix them. Pile them names up. Put one in the middle, date side up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Split First?. Here you set up the cousin cards and start the time line.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to place the top card in the line without turning it. 2. The player says a reason. 3. Turn the card over and check. 4. A wrongly placed card is moved and earns one mark.
flow.say: Where does this one go? Tell me your reason before you turn the card over.
flow.kid: Put your card in the line where you think it belongs. Say why. Then turn it over.

ask.q: The dog, the cow, the bat and the whale all have the same date. Why?
good: They are all on one branch.
That branch split from our branch once, so the date is the same for all of them.

flow.parent: Good reasons use features: 'A frog has four legs like us, and a fish does not, so the frog is closer.' The dates are middle values from the TimeTree database. The oldest ones are very uncertain.
flow.context: This is the main part of Who Split First?. Here you place each cousin card in the time line and check the date.

flow.do: 1. Count the marks. 2. Look along the finished line together. 3. Ask the check question. 4. Ask which card surprised your child most.
flow.say: Look along the line. Which card surprised you most? What is odd about the dates at the far right?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Look along the line. Which card surprised you most?

check.q: A rohu and a shark are both fish. Who is the rohu's closer relative: a shark or you?
options: You
The shark
Both equally
check.why: The rohu's line and the human line split about 435 million years ago. The shark's line had left earlier, about 460 million years ago. So a rohu shares a more recent ancestor with you than with a shark. If you chose 'the shark', you were sorting by shape and by living in water. 'Fish' is a way of life, not one branch.

flow.parent: The dates at the far right have very wide ranges. Say so. The older the split, the less sure the clock.
flow.context: This is the last step of Who Split First?. Here you look along the whole time line of your relatives.

games.title: Tree Talk: true or false by the tree?
games.context: This is a card game about reading family trees correctly. You draw one tree of six animals. Each card makes a claim about the tree. You say whether the tree supports the claim, and why.

printables.title: The tree to draw
items: Draw this bracket tree as a large fork diagram: (((((human, chimpanzee), gorilla), orangutan), bonnet macaque), rat).
Write the dates on the forks, from the top down: 6.5, 8.7, 15.6, 29 and 84 million years ago.

printables.title: 16 claim cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Humans descended from chimpanzees.
items.b: FALSE. Both descended from an ancestor who was neither, about 6.5 million years ago.

items.f: A gorilla is a closer relative of a chimpanzee than of a human.
items.b: FALSE. The gorilla's line joins below the fork that humans and chimpanzees share. So the gorilla is equally related to both.

items.f: A chimpanzee is a closer relative of a human than of a gorilla.
items.b: TRUE. The chimpanzee shares a fork with the human at 6.5 million years. The fork with the gorilla is older, at 8.7.

items.f: The rat is the oldest species on this tree.
items.b: FALSE. Every living tip is the same age. The rat's line has been changing for as long as ours.

items.f: The rat's line split off before any of the other lines here.
items.b: TRUE. The lowest fork, at 84 million years, separates the rat's line from all the others.

items.f: If you flip the top fork, so the chimpanzee is written first, the tree changes.
items.b: FALSE. Any fork can be flipped. The same members still share each fork.

items.f: An orangutan is equally related to a human, a chimpanzee and a gorilla.
items.b: TRUE. The orangutan's line joins below all three, at 15.6 million years.

items.f: Humans are the most evolved animal on this tree.
items.b: FALSE. All six lines have been evolving for the same length of time since the lowest fork.

items.f: The ancestor at the 8.7 fork was a gorilla.
items.b: FALSE. That ancestor was neither a gorilla, a chimpanzee nor a human. All three have changed since.

items.f: Human, chimpanzee and gorilla together, with their shared ancestor, make a clade.
items.b: TRUE. One snip below the 8.7 fork removes exactly these three.

items.f: Chimpanzee, gorilla and orangutan together, without the human, make a clade.
items.b: FALSE. No single snip removes those three and leaves the human. The human line is inside their branch.

items.f: A bonnet macaque is a closer relative of an orangutan than of a rat.
items.b: TRUE. Macaque and orangutan share a fork at 29 million years. The fork with the rat is at 84.

items.f: The tree shows that rats turned into monkeys, and monkeys into apes.
items.b: FALSE. A tree shows splits. No living tip turned into another living tip.

items.f: Two tips drawn next to each other are always the closest relatives.
items.b: FALSE. Only the forks count. A flipped fork puts different tips side by side.

items.f: The human line and the rat line have had the same time to change since they split.
items.b: TRUE. Both have had about 84 million years.

items.f: The date on a fork is exact.
items.b: FALSE. Each date is the middle of a range. For 6.5, studies give about 6.2 to 6.7.

rules: Draw the tree from the bracket line and write the dates on the forks. Put the tree where everyone can see.
Shuffle the 16 claim cards and pile them with the claims facing up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say 'true' or 'false', and point to the fork on the tree that shows it.
Turn the card over. If you were right and pointed to a fork that shows it, keep the card. If not, the card goes to the bottom of the pile.
The game ends when the pile is finished, or after 15 minutes. The player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: try to keep 13 of the 16 cards on the first time through.

setup.caption: 2. Read a claim. Say true or false, and point to the fork that shows it.

flow.say: True or false? Show me on the tree which fork tells you.
flow.kid: Read the card. Say true or false. Point to the fork that shows it. Then turn the card over.

ask.q: Why is a gorilla equally related to a human and a chimpanzee?
good: The gorilla's line joins below their shared fork.
The same ancestor links the gorilla to both.

flow.parent: The hardest cards are about the gorilla and the orangutan. Trace with a finger from each tip down to where the lines meet.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards. 2. Lay out the cards that were wrong first time. 3. Ask what they have in common. 4. Ask the check question.
