check.q: A rat and a human are both alive today. Which sentence is right?
options: Their lines have changed for equally long
The rat is an earlier stage of the human
The rat's line stopped changing long ago
check.why: After the split about 84 million years ago, each line kept on changing, in different directions. Neither is an earlier stage of the other. If you chose 'an earlier stage', you were reading the tree as a ladder. A tree has no top rung.

flow.parent: Most wrong answers come from one of two habits: reading the tips as a ladder, or judging by which tips are drawn side by side.
flow.context: This is the last step of Tree Talk. Here you look for the reading mistakes behind your wrong answers.

experiments.title: The Dice Clock Test: can chance mistakes tell time?
experiments.question: A strip of 30 squares stands for a gene. In each round a die decides, by chance, whether one square changes. If you roll for 10, 20 and 40 rounds, do the changes add up steadily enough to work as a clock? And can you use them to find out how many rounds a secret strip was rolled for?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Strip C is rolled for four times as many rounds as strip A. Will strip C end with about four times as many coloured squares, or will chance make the counts come out anyhow? Why do you think so? Then guess how close you will get to the secret number of rounds: within 5, within 10 or further off. Give your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Every strip has 30 squares. The same die is used, and a change happens only on a 5 or a 6. The chit always goes back into the tumbler, so every square has the same chance each time. Only one thing differs between the strips: the number of rounds.

materials.item: one die, from a ludo or snakes and ladders set
squared paper, or plain paper and a ruler
a steel tumbler to hold the chits
scissors
a pencil and one colour pencil or sketch pen

experiments.record: Draw the results table with four rows, for strips A, B, C and Mystery. For each strip write the rounds rolled, the number of coloured squares and the number of dots. Below the table write the rate you worked out and your estimate for the Mystery strip.
experiments.context: In this experiment a paper strip of 30 squares stands for a gene, and a die stands for chance. You roll for 10, 20 and 40 rounds and count how many squares have changed. Then you use your counts as a clock, to work out how long a secret strip was rolled for.

setup.art: Four paper strips of 30 numbered squares labelled A, B, C and Mystery, beside a steel tumbler full of small numbered chits and one die.
setup.caption: 1. Rule four strips of 30 squares. Put chits numbered 1 to 30 in a tumbler.

setup.art: A child's hand rolling a die that shows a six, with the other hand reaching into the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die. On a 5 or a 6, draw a chit.

setup.art: A child colouring in square number 14 on a strip while holding a chit marked 14.
setup.caption: 3. Colour the square with that number. Put the chit back.

setup.art: Three finished strips one above another, with 3, 7 and 11 squares coloured, and a count written at the end of each.
setup.caption: 4. Roll 10 rounds for A, 20 for B and 40 for C. Count the coloured squares.

setup.art: A grown-up rolling a die behind a propped-up book while a child looks away, with a folded slip of paper beside the grown-up.
setup.caption: 5. A grown-up rolls a secret number of rounds on the Mystery strip.

flow.do: 1. Your child cuts 30 small chits and numbers them 1 to 30. 2. They put the chits in the tumbler. 3. They rule four strips, each 30 squares long. 4. They number the squares 1 to 30 and label the strips A, B, C and Mystery.
flow.say: Each strip is one gene, and each square is one DNA letter. A coloured square will mean that letter has changed from the ancestor's letter.
flow.kid: Cut 30 chits and number them. Rule four strips of 30 squares. Label them A, B, C and Mystery.
flow.parent: Squares about 1 centimetre wide are easy to colour. If you have no squared paper, rule lines 1 centimetre apart.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dice Clock Test. Here you make the strips and the numbered chits.

flow.do: 1. Explain the rule of one round, given in the note below. 2. Ask for both guesses and the reasons. 3. Write them down.
flow.say: One round is one roll. On a 5 or a 6, one square changes. Strip C gets four times as many rounds as strip A. Will C have about four times as many coloured squares? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess: will strip C have four times as many coloured squares as A? Say why. Write your guess.

ask.q: Each roll is pure chance. Do you think the totals will be regular or anyhow? Why?
good: Chance is random, so the totals could be anything.
Over many rolls the 5s and 6s should even out, so more rounds should give more changes.

flow.parent: The rule of one round: roll the die. On 1, 2, 3 or 4, nothing happens. On 5 or 6, draw a chit, colour that square and put the chit back. Do not say which guess is right. Many children expect chance to give no pattern at all.
flow.context: In this step of the Dice Clock Test you guess whether chance changes will add up evenly, before you roll.

flow.do: 1. Your child rolls 10 rounds for strip A, making a tally mark for each round. 2. On a 5 or a 6 they draw a chit and colour that square on strip A. 3. The chit goes back in the tumbler each time. 4. If the square is already coloured, they put a small dot in it.
flow.say: Ten rounds for strip A. Keep a tally so you do not lose count. If a chit comes up twice, put a dot in the square. That is a second change at the same place.
flow.kid: Roll 10 rounds for strip A. On a 5 or 6, draw a chit. Colour that square. Put the chit back.

check.q: In the Dice Clock Test, what does a roll of 5 or 6 stand for?
options: A copying mistake in the DNA
One year going by
An animal dying
check.why: A 5 or 6 stands for a mutation, which is a copying mistake that changes one letter. Every roll stands for time going by, whether or not anything changes. If you chose 'one year going by', notice that most rolls pass with no change at all.

flow.parent: Strip A usually ends with 2 to 4 coloured squares. It can end with 1, or with 5 or 6. Any of these is a real result.
flow.context: In this step of the Dice Clock Test you roll 10 rounds and colour the squares that change on strip A.

flow.do: 1. Your child rolls 20 rounds for strip B in the same way. 2. They roll 40 rounds for strip C. 3. They count the coloured squares and the dots on each strip. 4. They write all the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Now twenty rounds for strip B and forty for strip C. Count only the coloured squares. A scientist comparing two sequences cannot see the dots.
flow.kid: Roll 20 rounds for strip B. Roll 40 rounds for strip C. Count the coloured squares on each.
flow.parent: Strip B usually ends with 5 to 7 coloured squares, and strip C with 9 to 12. Take turns rolling if your child's arm gets tired. The tally marks matter: a miscount of rounds spoils the clock.
flow.context: In this step of the Dice Clock Test you roll 20 rounds for strip B and 40 rounds for strip C.

flow.do: 1. Your child adds the coloured squares on A, B and C. 2. They divide that total by 70, the total number of rounds. 3. They write the answer as the rate: coloured squares in each round. 4. Ask whether the counts rose in step with the rounds.
flow.say: You rolled 70 rounds in all. Add up your coloured squares and divide by 70. That is your clock's rate. Did twice the rounds give about twice the squares?
flow.kid: Add the coloured squares on A, B and C. Divide by 70. That is your clock's rate.

ask.q: Did strip C have exactly four times as many coloured squares as strip A? Why might it have fewer?
good: Not exactly, because the rolls are chance.
Some changes on C landed on squares that were already coloured, so they do not show.

flow.parent: With 21 coloured squares the rate is 21 ÷ 70 = 0.3 in each round. A calculator is fine. Your child has now calibrated a clock: the rate was set from strips whose rounds are known.
flow.context: In this step of the Dice Clock Test you work out the rate of your clock from the three strips whose rounds you know.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks away. 2. Choose a secret number of rounds between 15 and 45, and write it on a slip. 3. Roll that many rounds on the Mystery strip. 4. Colour the squares, but keep any dots as tally marks on your slip. 5. Hide the slip.
flow.say: Look away while I roll the Mystery strip. I will not tell you how many rounds I rolled.
flow.kid: Look away. A grown-up rolls a secret number of rounds on the Mystery strip.
flow.parent: If your child is working alone, they can ask anyone at home to do this step. If nobody is free, they use this ready-made Mystery strip: 9 coloured squares. The secret number is given in the next step's note.
flow.context: In this step of the Dice Clock Test a grown-up rolls a secret number of rounds on the Mystery strip.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts the coloured squares on the Mystery strip. 2. They divide that count by their rate to estimate the rounds. 3. They write the estimate. 4. Show the hidden slip. 5. They write how far off the estimate was.
flow.say: Count the coloured squares on the Mystery strip. Divide by your rate. How many rounds do you think I rolled? Now look at my slip.
flow.kid: Count the coloured squares on the Mystery strip. Divide by your rate. Then check the secret slip.
flow.parent: For example, 9 coloured squares ÷ 0.3 = 30 rounds. The ready-made strip was rolled for 34 rounds. About three times in four, the estimate lands within 10 rounds of the truth. A miss by more than 10 is also a real result. Ask what could make the estimate better.
flow.context: In this step of the Dice Clock Test you use your rate to estimate how many rounds the Mystery strip was rolled for, and then check.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Could you have predicted any single roll?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Your estimate was not exactly right. What would make a clock like this more exact?
good: More rounds and more squares, so chance evens out more.
Using several strips and taking the average.
Setting the rate from more strips.

ask.q: Why does a scientist give a range, such as '25 to 35', and not one number?
good: Because the changes come by chance, so the count wobbles.
Because the rate is only an average.

flow.parent: The explanation: no single roll can be predicted, but about one roll in three gives a 5 or a 6. Over many rolls the changes pile up at close to that average rate. So the count of changes rises roughly in step with the rounds, and can be read backwards as a time. DNA works in the same way, with copying mistakes in place of rolls. Three things are simplified here. You compared each strip with the starting strip. Scientists never have the ancestor's DNA, so they compare two living species, and the changes in both lines add up. Real DNA has four letters, so a place can change back. And real rates are far lower: most letters do not change in a million years.
flow.think: If you rolled a strip for 500 rounds, nearly every square would be coloured. What could your clock tell you then?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Dice Clock Test. You say what your counts show about chance and time.

experiments.title: Fast Gene, Slow Gene: is a faster clock always a better clock?
experiments.question: Two strips of 12 squares stand for two genes. The fast gene changes on a roll of 3, 4, 5 or 6. The slow gene changes only on a 6. Which gene is the better clock for a short time, and which for a long time?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After 6 rounds, which strip will tell you more? After 48 rounds, which strip will tell you more? Write both guesses, and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Both strips have 12 squares and use the same die and the same 12 chits. Both are rolled for the same rounds, and counted at rounds 6, 12, 24 and 48. Only one thing differs: how often a change happens.

materials.item: one die
chits numbered 1 to 12, from the Dice Clock Test
a steel tumbler
squared paper, a pencil and two colour pencils

experiments.record: Draw the results table with four rows, for rounds 6, 12, 24 and 48. At each stop, write the number of coloured squares on the fast strip and on the slow strip. Then draw both as lines on one chart.
experiments.context: In this experiment two paper strips stand for a gene that changes often and a gene that changes rarely. You roll both for 48 rounds and count the changed squares at four stops. The aim is to find out which gene measures short times well and which measures long times well.

setup.art: Two paper strips of 12 numbered squares, one labelled FAST and one labelled SLOW, with a die and a tumbler of 12 chits.
setup.caption: 1. Rule two strips of 12 squares. Label them Fast and Slow.

setup.art: A die showing a 4 beside the Fast strip, with a child colouring a square on that strip.
setup.caption: 2. Fast strip: a square changes on a 3, 4, 5 or 6.

setup.art: A die showing a 6 beside the Slow strip, with a child colouring a square on that strip.
setup.caption: 3. Slow strip: a square changes only on a 6.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for rounds 6, 12, 24 and 48, partly filled in.
setup.caption: 4. Stop at rounds 6, 12, 24 and 48. Count the coloured squares on each strip.

flow.do: 1. Your child rules two strips of 12 squares and numbers the squares. 2. They label one Fast and one Slow. 3. They put chits 1 to 12 in the tumbler. 4. They draw the results table.
flow.say: The fast gene can change freely. The slow gene does a job that almost any change would spoil, so changes rarely last.
flow.kid: Rule two strips of 12 squares. Label them Fast and Slow. Put chits 1 to 12 in the tumbler.
flow.parent: One round is two rolls: one for the fast strip and one for the slow strip. Use a different colour for each strip.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fast Gene, Slow Gene. Here you make one strip for each gene.

flow.do: 1. Ask which strip will tell more after 6 rounds, and why. 2. Ask which will tell more after 48 rounds, and why. 3. Write both guesses.
flow.say: A fast gene collects changes quickly. Is a faster clock always a better clock? What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: Which strip will tell you more after 6 rounds? After 48 rounds? Say why.

ask.q: What happens to a strip of 12 squares when it is hit many, many times?
good: It fills up.
New hits land on squares that are already coloured.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say the fast strip is better every time, because it gives more to count.
flow.context: In this step of Fast Gene, Slow Gene you guess which gene will be the better clock for short and for long times.

flow.do: 1. Your child rolls once for the fast strip. On 3, 4, 5 or 6 they draw a chit and colour that square. 2. They roll once for the slow strip. On a 6 they draw a chit and colour that square. 3. The chit goes back each time. 4. They stop after rounds 6 and 12 and write both counts.
flow.say: One roll for the fast strip, one roll for the slow strip. That is one round. Stop at round 6 and at round 12 to count.
flow.kid: Roll once for Fast and once for Slow. Colour the squares that change. Count at rounds 6 and 12.
flow.parent: After 6 rounds the fast strip usually has 3 or 4 coloured squares, and the slow strip 0, 1 or 2. Keep a tally of rounds.
flow.context: In this step of Fast Gene, Slow Gene you roll the first 12 rounds and count at rounds 6 and 12.

flow.do: 1. Your child carries on with the same two strips up to round 24, and writes both counts. 2. They carry on to round 48 and write both counts. 3. Take turns with the rolling.
flow.say: Keep going on the same strips. Count again at round 24 and at round 48.
flow.kid: Keep rolling on the same strips. Count at round 24. Count again at round 48.

check.q: A strip of 12 squares has 11 coloured. Why will the count now rise very slowly?
options: Most new hits land on coloured squares
The die has become tired
The slow rule has taken over
check.why: With 11 of 12 squares coloured, eleven hits in twelve land on a square that has already changed. Those are hidden changes, and the count does not go up. If you chose 'the slow rule', check the rule: the fast strip still changes on 3, 4, 5 or 6.

flow.parent: By round 24 the fast strip usually has 8 to 10 coloured squares. By round 48 it has 11 or 12. The slow strip usually has 2 to 4 at round 24, and 5 to 7 at round 48.
flow.context: In this step of Fast Gene, Slow Gene you roll on to round 48 and count at rounds 24 and 48.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a line chart with rounds along the bottom and coloured squares up the side. 2. They plot one line for each strip. 3. Ask what they thought, what they saw and why. 4. After they answer, read the explanation in the note.
flow.say: Draw both lines on one chart. Which line is still climbing at the end? Which strip could tell round 6 from round 12? Which could tell round 24 from round 48?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each strip. Which line is still climbing at the end? Say why.

ask.q: You want to date a split that happened very long ago. Which kind of gene do you choose, and why?
good: A slow gene, because it has not filled up.
A fast gene would be full of hidden changes.

ask.q: You want to tell apart two groups that split only recently. Which kind of gene, and why?
good: A fast gene, because the slow one has hardly changed yet.

flow.parent: The explanation: the fast strip separates short times well, because it soon has several changes to count. But it fills up, and after that it hardly moves. The slow strip shows almost nothing at first, and keeps climbing steadily over the long run. Real scientists choose in the same way. They use fast-changing DNA for recent splits, and slow genes, such as the genes for ribosome parts, for the oldest splits.
flow.think: Is there one gene that would be a good clock for every question?
flow.context: This is the last step of Fast Gene, Slow Gene. You compare the two lines and say which gene suits which question.

activities.title: Cousins by Looks: six guesses to keep
activities.context: In this activity you guess who is whose closer relative, using only what you know about how animals look and live. You write down your reasons. Then you see what scientists found, and ask how they could know.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write the numbers 1 to 6 down the page. Beside each, write your guess and one reason. Leave space to write the scientists' answer later.

setup.art: A notebook page with six numbered lines, the first reading 'Dolphin: shark or cow?' with a child's pencil circling 'shark'.
setup.caption: 1. Write a guess and a reason for each of the six questions.

setup.art: A dolphin in the middle with a shark on one side and a cow on the other, and a question mark above the dolphin.
setup.caption: 2. For each animal, pick the closer relative of the two.

setup.art: The same notebook page with a second column of answers and dates in millions of years.
setup.caption: 3. Write the scientists' answers beside your guesses.

flow.do: 1. Read out the first three questions from the note below. 2. Your child writes a guess and a reason for each. 3. Do not give any answers yet.
flow.say: For each animal I name, pick the closer relative of the two. Tell me your reason each time.
flow.kid: Who is the dolphin's closer relative: a shark or a cow? Who is the crow's: a bat or a crocodile? Who is the dugong's: a dolphin or an elephant? Write your guesses and reasons.
flow.parent: The questions. 1: a dolphin, is the closer relative a shark or a cow? 2: a crow, a flying fox bat or a crocodile? 3: a dugong, a dolphin or an elephant? A dugong is a large plant-eating sea mammal of Palk Bay, also called a sea cow.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cousins by Looks. Here you guess the closer relative of a dolphin, a crow and a dugong.

flow.do: 1. Read out the last three questions from the note below. 2. Your child writes a guess and a reason for each. 3. Ask what kind of clue they used most.
flow.say: Three more. What kind of clue did you use most: shape, where they live, or something else?
flow.kid: Who is the crocodile's closer relative: a garden lizard or a hen? Who is the bat's: a rat or a dog? Who is the hippo's: a pig or a whale? Write your guesses and reasons.
flow.parent: The questions. 4: a crocodile, a garden lizard or a hen? 5: a flying fox bat, a rat or a dog? 6: a hippo, a pig or a whale? Most children use body shape and the place where the animal lives.
flow.context: In this step of Cousins by Looks you guess the closer relative of a crocodile, a bat and a hippo.

flow.do: 1. Read out the answers in the note below, with the dates. 2. Your child writes them beside the guesses and counts the surprises. 3. Ask the question below, and leave it open.
flow.say: Here is what scientists found. How many surprised you? Nobody saw these family lines split. So how could anyone know who is closer, and when they parted?
flow.kid: Write the scientists' answers beside your guesses. Count your surprises. How could anyone know this?

check.q: A dugong is shaped like a dolphin but is a closer relative of an elephant. What does this show?
options: Body shape can follow the way of life
Elephants once lived in the sea
Scientists guess from where animals live
check.why: Animals who live in the same way often come to have the same shape, even when they are far apart on the family tree. A smooth body with flippers suits any large animal who swims. If you chose 'elephants once lived in the sea', notice that it was the dugong's ancestors who moved into the water.

flow.parent: The answers, with dates from the TimeTree database. 1: the cow. Dolphin and cow split about 57 million years ago, dolphin and shark about 460 million. 2: the crocodile, at about 243 million years. Crow and bat split about 319 million years ago. 3: the elephant, at about 61 million years. Dugong and dolphin split about 97 million years ago. 4: the hen, at about 243 million years, against about 281 million for the lizard. 5: the dog, at about 79 million years, against about 89 million for the rat. 6: the whale, at about 53 million years, against about 59 million for the pig. Keep the page. The rest of the unit answers the question.
flow.context: This is the last step of Cousins by Looks. Here you compare your guesses with what scientists found.

activities.title: Fewest Changes: three possible trees for a shark, a dolphin and a cow
activities.context: In this activity you test three possible family trees for a shark, a dolphin and a cow. For each tree you count how many times features would have had to appear. The tree that needs the fewest changes is the scientists' first choice.

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: Draw the feature table. Draw the three trees. Under each tree write the number of changes it needs, and circle the smallest.

chart.title: The feature table. An earthworm, the outsider, has none of these features.
rows: 2. Mother feeds the young on milk
3. Has hair at some time in life
4. Keeps the whole body warm inside
5. Front limb bones: one, then two, then many
6. Three tiny bones in each middle ear
8. Lives the whole of life in the sea

setup.art: A notebook table with eight features down the side and three columns headed Shark, Dolphin and Cow, filled with 'yes' and 'no'.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the feature table.

setup.art: Three small fork diagrams in a row: one joining dolphin and cow first, one joining dolphin and shark first, one joining shark and cow first.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the three possible trees.

setup.art: One of the trees with small tick marks on the branches and the sum '6 + 4 = 10' written below.
setup.caption: 3. Count the changes each tree needs. Circle the smallest total.

flow.do: 1. Your child copies the feature table into the notebook. 2. Talk through each feature, using the note below. 3. Ask which features only the dolphin and the cow share. 4. Ask which only the dolphin and the shark share.
flow.say: An earthworm has none of these eight features. So each one is a new feature that appeared somewhere on this tree. Which features do the dolphin and the cow share? Which do the dolphin and the shark share?
flow.kid: Copy the feature table. Which features do the dolphin and cow share? Which do the dolphin and shark share?
flow.parent: A dolphin's flipper holds the same bones as a cow's front leg and your arm: one upper bone, two lower bones, then many small ones. Dolphin calves are born with a few whiskers. A few large sharks keep some muscles warm, but not the whole body as mammals do.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fewest Changes. Here you fill in a table of eight features for a shark, a dolphin and a cow.

flow.do: 1. Explain that any two of the three could be the sisters. 2. Your child draws three trees. 3. They label them: Tree 1 with dolphin and cow as sisters, Tree 2 with dolphin and shark, Tree 3 with shark and cow.
flow.say: On each tree, two of the animals share a fork and the third joins lower down. Draw all three trees. Which do you think is right, and why?
flow.kid: Draw three trees. Each has a different pair of sisters. Which tree do you think is right?
flow.parent: As bracket trees these are ((dolphin, cow), shark), ((dolphin, shark), cow) and ((shark, cow), dolphin).
flow.context: In this step of Fewest Changes you draw the three possible trees for a shark, a dolphin and a cow.

flow.do: 1. Give the counting rule from the note below. 2. Your child takes Tree 1 and goes down the table, one feature at a time. 3. They write 1 or 2 beside each feature and add up.
flow.say: Here is the rule. If the two animals with a feature are sisters on this tree, the feature appeared once. That is 1 change. If they are not sisters, that is 2 changes.
flow.kid: Take Tree 1. For each feature write 1 if the two owners are sisters. Write 2 if not. Add up.
flow.parent: Why 2 changes? Either the feature appeared twice, or it appeared once lower down and was then lost once. Both ways cost two changes. Tree 1: features 1 to 6 cost 1 each, and features 7 and 8 cost 2 each. 6 + 4 = 10.
flow.context: In this step of Fewest Changes you count the changes that the first tree needs.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts Tree 2 and Tree 3 in the same way. 2. They circle the tree with the smallest total. 3. Ask what the winning tree says about the fish shape.
flow.say: Count the other two trees. Which tree needs the fewest changes? On that tree, how many times did the fish shape appear?
flow.kid: Count Tree 2 and Tree 3. Circle the smallest total. How many times did the fish shape appear?
flow.parent: Tree 2: features 7 and 8 cost 1 each, and features 1 to 6 cost 2 each. 2 + 12 = 14. Tree 3: all eight cost 2 each, which is 16. Tree 1 wins with 10. On Tree 1 the fish shape appeared twice, once in sharks and once in dolphins. It is a lookalike feature.
flow.context: In this step of Fewest Changes you count the other two trees and choose the tree with the smallest total.

flow.do: 1. Cover features 1 to 6 with a hand, so only features 7 and 8 show. 2. Ask which tree would win now. 3. Ask what that says about using only a few features.
flow.say: Suppose you had seen only the last two features. Which tree would win? What does that tell you about how many features a scientist should use?
flow.kid: Cover features 1 to 6. Which tree wins with only two features? What does that tell you?

check.q: Two possible trees need 10 changes and 14 changes. Why do scientists try the 10-change tree first?
options: A big feature rarely evolves twice
Smaller numbers are easier to remember
The first tree drawn is usually right
check.why: A feature such as milk needs many genes to change over a long time. That is much less likely to happen twice than once, so the tree with fewer repeats is the better first choice. If you chose 'easier to remember', think again about what each change stands for: a real event in a real family line.

flow.parent: With only features 7 and 8, Tree 2 wins, and the dolphin goes with the shark. That is the mistake people made for centuries. More features make a lookalike easier to catch.
flow.think: Your eyes and an octopus's eyes work in a similar way. Would you count that as a shared new feature or a lookalike? How could you find out?
flow.context: This is the last step of Fewest Changes. Here you find out what happens when a tree is built from too few features.

activities.title: The Whale Case: four pieces of evidence, in the order they arrived
activities.context: In this activity you follow a real case. For over thirty years scientists asked who the whale's closest relatives are. You hear four pieces of evidence in the order they were found. After each one you say which relative you would pick, and how sure you are.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw four rows, for 1966, 1997, 2001 and 2007. In each row write the relative you would pick, and how sure you are from 1 (a guess) to 5 (very sure).

setup.art: A notebook with four rows labelled 1966, 1997, 2001 and 2007, and two columns headed 'My pick' and 'How sure, 1 to 5'.
setup.caption: 1. Draw four rows, one for each piece of evidence.

setup.art: A fossil jaw with pointed three-part teeth beside a second, similar jaw, both with labels.
setup.caption: 2. Hear each piece of evidence. Start with the teeth.

setup.art: A small ankle bone shaped like a double pulley, drawn large beside the foot of a deer.
setup.caption: 3. After each one, write your pick and how sure you are.

flow.do: 1. Read out the 1966 evidence from the note below. 2. Your child writes a pick and a number from 1 to 5 for how sure they are. 3. Ask what could change their mind.
flow.say: It is 1966. All you have are fossil teeth. Who do you pick as the whale's relatives, and how sure are you from 1 to 5?
flow.kid: It is 1966. You have only fossil teeth. Write your pick. How sure are you, from 1 to 5?
flow.parent: 1966, teeth. The earliest fossil whales have pointed teeth with three parts. They look very much like the teeth of mesonychids, extinct meat-eating hoofed mammals about the size of a wolf. Leigh Van Valen proposed that whales came from mesonychids.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Whale Case. Here you judge the oldest evidence, which is fossil teeth.

flow.do: 1. Read out the 1997 evidence from the note below. 2. Your child writes a new pick and a new number. 3. Ask whether teeth or DNA should count for more, and why.
flow.say: It is 1997. Now there is DNA, and it disagrees with the teeth. What is your pick now? Which evidence do you trust more, and why?
flow.kid: It is 1997. The DNA disagrees with the teeth. Write your new pick. How sure are you now?

ask.q: Why is the same jumping gene at the same place such strong evidence?
good: It would almost never land in the same place twice by chance.
So both must have got it from one ancestor.

flow.parent: 1997, DNA. Through the 1990s, DNA comparisons kept placing whales inside the even-toed hoofed mammals, next to hippos. In 1997 a Japanese team found the same jumping genes at the same places in whales, hippos and cattle. Many fossil experts still doubted it, because no fossil whale had a hoofed animal's bones.
flow.context: In this step of the Whale Case you judge the DNA evidence, which disagreed with the teeth.

flow.do: 1. Read out the 2001 evidence from the note below. 2. Your child writes a new pick and a new number. 3. Ask why a third kind of evidence helped.
flow.say: It is 2001. Two teams have found early whales with legs, and the ankle bones are there. What is your pick now? Why does a third kind of evidence matter?
flow.kid: It is 2001. Early whales with legs are found. Their ankles match hippos and deer. Write your pick.
flow.parent: 2001, ankles. Two teams working in Pakistan found skeletons of early whales with legs. One team was led by Philip Gingerich and the other by Hans Thewissen. The ankle bone had a double-pulley shape, rounded at both ends. Only even-toed hoofed mammals, such as hippos, cattle, deer and pigs, have that ankle. Mesonychids do not. Gingerich had supported the mesonychid idea, and he changed his mind.
flow.context: In this step of the Whale Case you judge fossil ankle bones, which agreed with the DNA.

flow.do: 1. Read out the 2007 evidence from the note below. 2. Your child writes a last pick and number. 3. Look back down the four rows together. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at your four rows. When did your pick change, and what changed it? Were the scientists of 1966 foolish?
flow.kid: Hear the 2007 find from Kashmir. Write your last pick. Look at your four rows. What changed your mind?

check.q: Early whales had teeth like mesonychids but ankles like hippos and deer. What were the teeth?
options: A lookalike feature
A shared new feature
A copying mistake
check.why: Meat-eating mammals of several kinds have evolved similar pointed teeth, because the teeth do the same job. So the teeth were a lookalike. The ankle is an odd shape with no link to diet, and DNA agreed with it. If you chose 'a shared new feature', remember that two other kinds of evidence pointed away from mesonychids.

flow.parent: 2007, an ear from Kashmir. The geologist A. Ranga Rao had collected fossil-bearing rocks at Kalakot in Kashmir years before. After his death, his widow gave the rocks to Hans Thewissen. A skull broke during cleaning and showed a thick ear bone known only from whales. The animal, Indohyus, was a deer-like wader the size of a fox. Sunil Bajpai and B. N. Tiwari were among the Indian scientists on the team. The scientists of 1966 reasoned well from what they had. Teeth were the only evidence then.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Whale Case. Here you add a fossil from Kashmir and look back at how your answer changed.

activities.title: Bracket Trees: same tree or different tree?
activities.context: In this activity you learn to write a family tree in one line, using brackets. Then you test pairs of trees to see whether they are the same tree drawn differently, or two different trees.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw each bracket tree as a fork diagram. For the five pairs, write 'same' or 'different' and one reason.

setup.art: The words '((me, my sister), my cousin)' with a fork diagram drawn below: two tips joined first, and a third joining lower down.
setup.caption: 1. One pair of brackets is one fork. The two things inside are sisters.

setup.art: A fork diagram of a crow, a crocodile and a lizard, with a curved arrow showing the top fork being flipped.
setup.caption: 2. Flipping a fork does not change the tree.

setup.art: Two bracket trees written side by side with a question mark between them, and a child's pencil writing 'same'.
setup.caption: 3. For each pair, check who shares a fork with whom.

flow.do: 1. Write ((me, my sister), my cousin) on the page. 2. Explain that each pair of brackets is one fork. 3. Your child draws it as a fork diagram. 4. Ask who the inner brackets hold, and why.
flow.say: The inner brackets hold the two who are closest. The outer brackets add the next closest. Draw this as a tree with two forks.
flow.kid: Each pair of brackets is one fork. Draw ((me, my sister), my cousin) as a tree.
flow.parent: If your child has no sister or cousin, use any three relatives or friends from one family. Scientists really do write trees this way for computers.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bracket Trees. Here you learn how brackets stand for the forks of a family tree.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws these three bracket trees as fork diagrams. 2. First: ((crow, crocodile), lizard). 3. Second: (((human, chimpanzee), gorilla), orangutan). 4. Third: ((whale, hippo), (cow, deer)).
flow.say: Draw each one. Start from the innermost brackets and work outward.
flow.kid: Draw three trees from brackets. Start with the innermost brackets each time.
flow.parent: The third tree has two inner pairs. Each pair is a fork, and then the two forks join.
flow.context: In this step of Bracket Trees you turn three bracket trees into fork diagrams.

flow.do: 1. Read out the five pairs in the note below, one at a time. 2. For each pair, your child lists who is inside each pair of brackets. 3. They write 'same' or 'different'.
flow.say: Two trees are the same if every fork holds the same members. The order inside a pair of brackets does not matter. Same or different?
flow.kid: For each pair of trees, check who shares each fork. Write 'same' or 'different'.
flow.parent: The pairs. 1: ((crow, crocodile), lizard) and (lizard, (crocodile, crow)). Same. 2: ((human, chimpanzee), gorilla) and ((chimpanzee, gorilla), human). Different. 3: ((whale, hippo), cow) and (cow, (hippo, whale)). Same. 4: ((tomato, potato), brinjal) and ((tomato, brinjal), potato). Different. 5: (((human, chimpanzee), gorilla), orangutan) and (orangutan, (gorilla, (chimpanzee, human))). Same.
flow.context: In this step of Bracket Trees you decide whether five pairs of trees are the same tree or different trees.

flow.do: 1. Ask the check question. 2. Ask your child to write the ape tree with the tips in a new order, without changing the tree.
flow.say: Write the ape tree again so that the human is not at either end. It must still be the same tree.
flow.kid: Write the ape tree with the tips in a new order. Keep it the same tree.

check.q: On the tree (((human, chimpanzee), gorilla), orangutan), who is the gorilla's closer relative?
options: Human and chimpanzee, equally
The chimpanzee
The orangutan
check.why: The gorilla's line joins the tree at the fork below the human and chimpanzee pair. So the gorilla shares the same ancestor with both, and is equally related to each. If you chose 'the chimpanzee', you may have judged by which name is written nearer. Only the forks count.

flow.parent: One answer is (orangutan, ((chimpanzee, human), gorilla)). Any order is fine if the same members sit inside each pair of brackets.
flow.context: This is the last step of Bracket Trees. Here you check that the order of the tips does not change who is related to whom.

activities.title: The Brinjal Family on a Ruler: a time tree from the kitchen
activities.context: In this activity you look inside a tomato, a brinjal and a chilli, and compare them with a potato. All four belong to one plant family. Then you draw their family tree to scale, so that each fork shows how long ago the lines split.

materials.item: one tomato, one small brinjal, one green chilli and one potato
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a sheet of plain paper turned sideways, a 30-centimetre ruler and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Wash hands after touching the cut chilli, and keep fingers away from the eyes.
activities.record: Draw what you see inside each cut vegetable. Then draw the time tree, with each fork at the right distance from the 'today' edge.

setup.art: A tomato, a brinjal and a green chilli each cut across, showing seeds attached to a pale central part, with a whole potato beside them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the tomato, the brinjal and the chilli across.

setup.art: A sheet of paper turned sideways with a ruler along the bottom, the right-hand edge labelled 'today', and four names written down that edge.
setup.caption: 2. Write the four names down the right-hand edge. That edge is today.

setup.art: A tree drawn sideways on the paper with forks at 8.5, 15.8 and 21 centimetres from the right-hand edge.
setup.caption: 3. Draw each fork at its distance. One centimetre is one million years.

flow.do: 1. Cut the tomato, the brinjal and the chilli across the middle. 2. Your child looks at how the seeds are attached inside each. 3. They draw the three cut faces. 4. Show the potato and ask where the seeds are.
flow.say: Look at where the seeds sit in each one. What is the same in all three? Now look at the potato. Where are the seeds?
flow.kid: Look inside the tomato, the brinjal and the chilli. Draw where the seeds sit. What is the same?
flow.parent: In all three, many flat seeds are attached to a pale central part. The potato we eat is a swollen underground stem, so there are no seeds inside. A potato plant does make small green fruits like tiny tomatoes. They are poisonous and are never eaten.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Brinjal Family on a Ruler. Here you look inside three fruits of one plant family.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that all four plants belong to one family. 2. Ask them to guess which two are the closest relatives, and why. 3. Write the guess as a bracket tree.
flow.say: These four are one family. Which two do you think are the closest relatives? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which two of the four are closest relatives. Say why. Write your guess.
flow.parent: Most children pair the tomato with the brinjal or the chilli, because the potato grows underground.
flow.context: In this step of the Brinjal Family on a Ruler you guess the family tree of four kitchen plants.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns the paper sideways and writes the four names down the right-hand edge, in this order: tomato, potato, brinjal, chilli. 2. They measure back from that edge. 3. They join tomato and potato at 8.5 centimetres. 4. They join brinjal to that pair at 15.8 centimetres. 5. They join chilli at 21 centimetres.
flow.say: The right-hand edge is today. One centimetre is one million years. The tomato and potato lines meet 8.5 centimetres back. The brinjal joins at 15.8 centimetres, and the chilli at 21.
flow.kid: Join tomato and potato 8.5 centimetres back. Join brinjal at 15.8 centimetres. Join chilli at 21 centimetres.
flow.parent: The dates are middle values from the TimeTree database: about 8.5, 15.8 and 21 million years. Each has a range of a few million years either way. As a bracket tree this is (((tomato, potato), brinjal), chilli).
flow.context: In this step of the Brinjal Family on a Ruler you draw the family tree of four kitchen plants to scale.

flow.do: 1. Your child compares the tree with their guess. 2. Ask the check question. 3. Ask what the tomato and potato ancestor might have looked like.
flow.say: Was your guess right? Look at your tree. Is the brinjal closer to the tomato or to the potato?
flow.kid: Compare the tree with your guess. Is the brinjal closer to the tomato or the potato?

check.q: On the tree (((tomato, potato), brinjal), chilli), is the brinjal closer to the tomato or the potato?
options: Equally close to both
Closer to the tomato
Closer to the potato
check.why: The brinjal's line joins below the fork that the tomato and the potato share. So the brinjal's last shared ancestor with the tomato is the very same one as with the potato, about 15.8 million years ago. If you chose 'the tomato', you may have been thinking of how alike the fruits look.

flow.parent: The surprise is that the potato, with a different-looking edible part, is the tomato's closest relative here. The part people eat says little about the family.
flow.think: A tomato and you are relatives too. On this scale, the fork would be about 14.5 metres to the left of your paper. Why so far?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Brinjal Family on a Ruler. Here you read your time tree and compare it with your guess.

projects.title: Ten Neighbours on One Time Tree
projects.context: In this three-day project you choose ten living beings that share your home and street with you. You work out their family tree, look up when their lines split, and draw the whole tree to scale on a long strip of paper.

materials.item: old newspaper sheets taped end to end to make a strip 80 centimetres long
a ruler or measuring tape, a pencil and colour pencils
a phone or computer with a grown-up, for the TimeTree website
a notebook

schedule.what: List ten living beings seen from home, with yourself as one of them. Write a first bracket tree from what you know.
With a grown-up, look up the split dates on timetree.org. Correct your bracket tree.
Draw the tree to scale on the long strip, with 1 centimetre for 20 million years. Show it to your family.

projects.record: A notebook page with your list, your first bracket tree and your corrected one. A table of split dates. The finished strip.

setup.art: A child at a window writing a list: crow, pigeon, house gecko, ant, street dog, cat, squirrel, coconut tree, mushroom, me.
setup.caption: 1. List ten living neighbours, with yourself as one.

setup.art: A phone screen showing two name boxes and a result reading '319 MYA', held by a grown-up beside a child with a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Look up when each pair of lines split.

setup.art: A long strip of taped newspaper on the floor with a tree drawn along it, the right-hand end labelled 'today' and forks marked with dates.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the tree to scale along a long strip.

flow.do: 1. Your child lists ten living beings they can see from home, with themselves as one. 2. They include at least one plant, one insect and one bird. 3. They group the closest ones in brackets, then add the others. 4. They write one reason for each fork.
flow.say: Who lives around us? Choose ten, and count yourself. Which two are the closest relatives? Put them in brackets first. What feature tells you?
flow.kid: List ten living neighbours. Count yourself as one. Put the closest two in brackets first. Give a reason.
flow.parent: A list that works in most flats: crow, pigeon, house gecko, ant, mosquito, street dog, cat, a potted tulsi or a coconut tree, mould on old bread, and the child. A good first tree puts crow with pigeon, dog with cat, and ant with mosquito.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Ten Neighbours on One Time Tree. Here you choose ten living beings and write a first family tree.

flow.do: 1. Open timetree.org and choose the tool that compares two species. 2. Type two names from the list, such as 'dog' and 'cat'. 3. Your child writes the middle date and the range. 4. Repeat for each fork of the bracket tree. 5. They correct the tree where the dates disagree with it.
flow.say: Type two names and read the date. A smaller number means a more recent split. Does the date fit your tree? If not, change the brackets.
flow.kid: Look up two names at a time. Write the date and the range. Fix your tree if the dates disagree.

ask.q: The website gives a range as well as one number. Why?
good: Different studies give different dates.
The clock counts chance changes, so the answer wobbles.

flow.parent: If a common name is not found, try the scientific name from a quick search. With no internet, use these dates in millions of years: dog and cat 54, crow and pigeon about 86, human and dog 89, bird and gecko 281, human and bird 319, ant and mosquito about 330, human and insect 720, human and mould 1,200, human and plant 1,450.
flow.context: This is day 2 of Ten Neighbours on One Time Tree. Here you look up when your neighbours' family lines split.

flow.do: 1. Your child lays the strip on the floor and labels the right-hand end 'today'. 2. They write the ten names down that end. 3. With 1 centimetre for 20 million years, they mark each fork at its distance. 4. They join the lines. 5. They show the family and name the most surprising pair.
flow.say: One centimetre is twenty million years. Divide each date by 20 to get the distance in centimetres. Which fork is the furthest back?
flow.kid: Divide each date by 20. Mark each fork that many centimetres back. Join the lines. Show your family.
flow.parent: On this scale the dog and cat fork is 2.7 centimetres back. The human and bird fork is about 16 centimetres back, and the plant fork is about 73 centimetres back. The recent forks crowd together at the right. That crowding is real: most of the tree's history lies before the animals we know appeared.
flow.context: This is day 3 of Ten Neighbours on One Time Tree. Here you draw the family tree of your neighbours to scale.

challenges.title: The Cousin Mobile: a hanging tree that stays true when it turns
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. A family tree drawn on paper is often misread, because people judge by which tips are side by side. Here you build the tree as a hanging mobile. Every fork can swing round, and the tree stays the same tree.
challenges.problem: Build a hanging mobile of six animals that shows who shares a fork with whom. It must hang level, and it must still show the right relatives after every stick is spun.
constraints: Use this tree: (((human, rat), ((crow, crocodile), lizard)), frog).
Each stick is one fork. Exactly two things hang from each stick: a name tag or another stick.
Use only home things: sticks from a coconut-leaf broom or straws, thread, paper and tape.
materials: five thin sticks from a coconut-leaf broom, or five paper straws
six paper tags and a pencil
a door handle or a hanger to hang the mobile from
general: Start from the bottom. Hang the crow tag and the crocodile tag from the two ends of one stick, and find the point where the stick hangs level.
Hang that stick from one end of a second stick, with the lizard tag at the other end. Slide the thread until it balances.
Use small paper tags and add a paper clip to a tag that is too light.
creative: Make each thread as long as the date of its fork, with 1 centimetre for 10 million years, so the mobile is also a time tree.
Draw each animal on both sides of the tag, so the mobile reads correctly from anywhere in the room.
Colour all the tags of one clade in one colour, and test whether one snip of the scissors would remove exactly that colour.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own mobile for six living beings of your choice. Write the bracket tree first. Build it and spin every stick. Ask someone at home who the frog's closest relatives are, and see whether they read your mobile correctly.

setup.art: A thin broom stick hanging level from a thread, with a paper tag reading 'crow' at one end and 'crocodile' at the other.
setup.caption: 1. Hang two sister tags from one stick. Find the point where the stick hangs level.

setup.art: A second stick above the first, with the first stick hanging from one end and a tag reading 'lizard' from the other.
setup.caption: 2. Hang that stick and the next relative from a new stick.

setup.art: A finished mobile of five sticks and six tags hanging from a door handle, with a child spinning one of the sticks.
setup.caption: 3. Build all five forks. Spin every stick and check the tree is unchanged.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the bracket tree as a fork diagram. 2. They count the forks. 3. They write the six name tags. 4. Ask how many sticks are needed, and why.
flow.say: Draw the tree first. Each fork will be one stick. How many sticks do you need?
flow.kid: Draw the tree from the brackets. Count the forks. Write six name tags.
flow.parent: There are five forks, so five sticks. From the top: frog and the rest, then the mammal pair and the reptile group, then human and rat, then lizard and the bird pair, then crow and crocodile.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cousin Mobile challenge. Here you plan the mobile from the bracket tree.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds from the lowest forks upward. 2. They tape a thread to each tag and tie the tags to the stick ends. 3. They slide the hanging thread along each stick until it hangs level. 4. They fix it with a small piece of tape.
flow.say: Build the smallest forks first: crow with crocodile, and human with rat. Slide the thread until each stick is level, then tape it.
flow.kid: Build the lowest forks first. Slide each thread until the stick hangs level. Tape it there.
flow.parent: Help with the scissors and the knots. A side with more hanging from it is heavier, so its thread sits nearer the middle. Balancing takes patience. A dab of tape holds the thread in place.
flow.context: In this step of the Cousin Mobile challenge you build the mobile from the lowest forks upward.

flow.do: 1. Hang the mobile from a door handle or a hanger. 2. Your child spins each stick in turn. 3. After each spin, they say who the crow's closest relative is. 4. Ask what changed and what did not.
flow.say: Spin any stick. Who is next to the crow now? Who is the crow's closest relative now? What changed, and what stayed the same?
flow.kid: Spin each stick. Who is next to the crow now? Who is the crow's closest relative?
flow.context: In this step of the Cousin Mobile challenge you spin the sticks and check that the relatives stay the same.

flow.do: 1. Ask the check question. 2. Your child chooses one idea from the creative list, or one of their own, and says how they would build it.
flow.say: What would you add to make your mobile show time as well as family?
flow.kid: Choose one way to make your mobile better. Say how you would build it.

check.q: On a hanging tree, a stick is spun so the crow now hangs beside the human. Has the crow's closest relative changed?
options: No, the crow still shares a stick with the crocodile
Yes, the human is closest now
Yes, whoever is nearest is closest
check.why: The closest relative is the one who shares the lowest stick, and spinning does not change which stick anything hangs from. If you chose 'whoever is nearest', that is the commonest mistake in reading a paper tree. The mobile shows why it is a mistake.

flow.parent: If the threads are made to scale, the crow and crocodile threads are about 24 centimetres long. Many families will prefer 1 centimetre for 20 million years.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cousin Mobile challenge. Here you check what spinning does and plan an improvement.

items.p: What decides how closely two living beings are related?
opts: How recently their family lines split
Whether they live in the same place
Whether they eat the same food
items.why: Relatives are close when their shared ancestor lived recently. Looks and homes can match in distant relatives. Choosing 'how alike they look' is the natural first guess, and the dolphin and the shark show why it fails.

items.p: On a family tree, each fork stands for a common ____.
items.why: A fork is the point where one family line became two. The population living at that point is the ancestor of everything above the fork.

items.p: True or false: humans descended from chimpanzees.
items.why: False. Humans and chimpanzees both descended from an ancestor who was neither. That ancestor lived about 6.5 million years ago, and both lines have changed since.

items.p: Match each animal or plant to their closest relative on the list.
items.why: Each pair was found from DNA, and fossils or body features agree. None of the pairs look alike at first sight.

items.p: Sort each likeness: a shared new feature, or a lookalike feature?
items.why: Milk, hair and the three ear bones were each inherited from one mammal ancestor. Wings and the fish shape evolved separately in groups that live in the same way.
items: Milk in a cow and a dolphin
Wings of a bat and a crow
Hair on a dog and a whale calf
Fish shape of a shark and a dolphin
Three ear bones in a rat and an elephant
Flippers of a dugong and a turtle

items.p: Two hand-copied notebooks are found. Which likeness best shows that one source lies behind both?
opts: The same rare mistake in the same place
items.why: A correct spelling could come from anywhere. A rare mistake in the same place is very unlikely to happen twice by chance, so one source is the best explanation. Scientists use shared rare changes in DNA in the same way.

items.p: Draw the bracket tree ((crow, crocodile), lizard) as a fork diagram. Mark the ancestor that the crow and the crocodile share.
items.a: A tree with two forks. The crow and the crocodile meet at the upper fork, which is marked. The lizard's line joins at the lower fork.
items.why: The inner brackets are the upper fork. A strong drawing marks that fork, and not the lower one, as the shared ancestor of the crow and the crocodile.
items.art: A blank space with the three names crow, crocodile and lizard written along the top.

items.p: True or false: flipping a fork on a family tree changes who is related to whom.
items.why: False. A flipped fork holds the same members. Only the order of the tips on the page changes, and that order carries no meaning.

items.p: In the Dice Clock Test, no roll could be predicted. Explain how the strips could still tell time.
items.a: About one roll in three gives a 5 or a 6. Over many rolls the changes add up at close to that rate. So the number of coloured squares rises roughly in step with the number of rounds, and can be read back as a time.
items.why: A strong answer separates one roll, which is chance, from many rolls, which have a steady average.

items.p: A strip gains 6 coloured squares in 20 rounds. What is the rate?
items.why: A rate is the amount divided by the time. 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3. Choosing 120 means multiplying where dividing was needed. Choosing 26 means adding.

items.p: Put the steps of using a molecular clock in order.
a: Count the DNA differences between two species
Find a split whose date is known from fossils
Work out the rate from that known split
Divide the differences by the rate to date the new split
items.why: The count comes first, and it is not yet a date. The rate has to be set against something known before the count can be turned into years.
items: Work out the rate from that known split
Divide the differences by the rate to date the new split
Count the DNA differences between two species
Find a split whose date is known from fossils

items.p: Three of these are shared new features of mammals. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Three bones in the middle ear
items.why: A backbone is much older than the mammals. Fish, frogs and birds have one too, so it cannot show which animals are mammals. The other three first appeared in the mammal line.

items.p: Setting a clock or a scale against something already known is called ____.
items.why: A molecular clock is calibrated with a split whose date is known. Without that step, a count of differences cannot be turned into years.

items.p: Label a family tree of three animals: tip, fork, branch, and the oldest fork.
a: Tip: the end of a line, a living group
Fork: where one line splits into two
Branch: the line between two forks, or from a fork to a tip
Oldest fork: the lowest one, shared by all three
items.why: The tips are the living groups. Every fork is a common ancestor, and the lowest fork is the ancestor of everyone on the tree.
items.art: A fork diagram of three animals drawn large, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Name one surprising pair of close relatives. Say what evidence shows they are close.
items.a: For example: whales and hippos. DNA puts them together, and they share jumping genes at the same places. Early fossil whales have the same double-pulley ankle bone as hippos, cattle and deer.
items.why: A strong answer names the pair and gives at least one piece of evidence that is not about looks.

items.p: Why do scientists give the date of a split as a range?
opts: The changes arrive by chance, so counts wobble
They have not tried hard enough
Dates are a matter of opinion
items.why: A count of chance events is never exactly the average, and the rate itself is an estimate. A range is the honest way to say how far off the date could be. Choosing 'a matter of opinion' misses that the range is worked out from the data.

worksheets.title: Fewest changes, fast and slow genes, and setting the clock (stretch)

items.p: On a possible tree, the two animals that share a feature are sisters. How many changes does that feature cost?
items.why: The feature needed to appear only once, in the ancestor the two sisters share. If the two were not sisters, it would cost two changes. Choosing 'none' forgets that the feature had to appear somewhere.

items.p: Two possible trees need 10 changes and 14 changes. Which do scientists try first, and why?
items.a: The tree with 10 changes. Each change is a real event, such as milk or lungs appearing. A big feature appearing twice in the same way is much less likely than appearing once. So the tree with fewer repeats is more likely.
items.why: A strong answer says what a change is, and why repeats are unlikely. It may add that the rule is a first choice and can be wrong when there are many lookalikes.

items.p: True or false: a dugong is a closer relative of a dolphin than of an elephant.
items.why: False. The dugong's line and the elephant's line split about 61 million years ago. The dugong's line and the dolphin's line split about 97 million years ago. The shared shape is a lookalike feature.

items.p: A fast-changing strip of 12 squares is nearly full. What can it no longer tell you?
opts: A long time from a very long time
items.why: Once nearly every square has changed, more rounds add almost nothing to the count. So 24 rounds and 48 rounds look alike. The strip still shows that plenty of time has passed.

items.p: Match each kind of evidence to what it is best used for.
items.why: Each tool suits a job. Fast DNA has enough changes to separate recent splits. Slow genes have not filled up over long times. A jumping gene at one place is a rare shared event. A dated fossil turns counts into years.
pairs: Telling apart groups that split recently
The same jumping gene at the same place
Showing two species share an ancestor
Setting the rate of the clock

items.p: A second change at a place that has already changed is called a ____ change.
items.why: Comparing two sequences shows only that the place differs. It cannot show how many times the place changed. Hidden changes make old splits look younger than they are.

items.p: It is 1997. Two scientists argue about the whale's closest relatives.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For example: the DNA scientist has the stronger case, because a jumping gene at the same place is very unlikely twice. It also says what the other has right: no fossil then showed a whale with a hoofed animal's bones, so asking for one was fair.
items.why: In 2001 the ankle bones were found and agreed with the DNA. Both scientists were reasoning well in 1997. The case was settled by a third kind of evidence.

views.says: Early whale teeth match mesonychid teeth. I trust bones I can hold.
Whales and hippos share jumping genes at the same places. That cannot be chance.

items.ask: Whose evidence is stronger in 1997? Give your reason. Then say one thing the other scientist has right.

items.p: Put these relatives of a hen in order, from closest to most distant.
items.why: The hen's line split from the crocodile's about 243 million years ago, the lizard's about 281, the mammals' about 319, the frog's about 352 and the rohu's about 435.

items.p: Draw the tree (((tomato, potato), brinjal), chilli). Circle the fork where the brinjal's line joins.
items.a: A tree with three forks, one above another. Tomato and potato meet at the top fork. The brinjal joins at the middle fork, which is circled. The chilli joins at the lowest fork.
items.why: The circled fork is the ancestor that the brinjal shares equally with the tomato and with the potato.
items.art: A blank space with the four names tomato, potato, brinjal and chilli written down the right-hand side.

items.p: Sort each group: a clade, or not a clade?
items.why: A clade is one ancestor with all the descendants. Birds, mammals, and whales with hippos each pass that test. Flyers and sea animals come from many separate branches. 'Fish' leaves out the land animals, who descend from fish.
items: Animals that live in the sea
Whales and hippos, with their shared ancestor

items.p: Two frog families split 131 million years ago. Their lands broke apart 65 million years ago. What follows?
opts: The families were separate before the land split
The land split caused the families to split
The frogs swam across the sea
items.why: 131 is older than 65. So the two families already existed while the land was one piece. When the land broke up, each piece carried one family away. Choosing 'the land split caused it' would need the two dates to match.

items.p: The oldest fossil of a branch is 50 million years old. Why might the branch be older than that?
items.a: Fossils form rarely, and few are found. The first members of the branch probably lived before the oldest fossil we happen to have. So the fossil shows the branch is at least 50 million years old, and it may be older.
items.why: A strong answer says the fossil gives the latest date by which the branch existed, not the date it began.

items.p: True or false: the oldest fossil of a branch shows the branch is at least that old.
items.why: True. If a member of the branch was alive then, the branch had already begun. The branch may be older, because earlier members may have left no fossils.

items.p: Three of these are on one branch of mammals that DNA revealed. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Elephants, dugongs and hyraxes belong to an old African branch called Afrotheria. The dolphin belongs with hippos, cattle and deer, on a different branch.

items.p: Two species differ in 2 letters per 100 and split 10 million years ago. When did a pair that differs in 6 split?
items.why: If the rate is the same, three times the differences means three times the time. 6 ÷ 2 = 3, and 3 × 10 = 30. Choosing 12 means adding 2 to 10 where multiplying was needed. These numbers are made up.

items.p: A rohu and a shark are both called fish. Explain why 'fish' is not one branch of the tree.
items.a: The rohu's line is closer to the line of frogs, birds and humans than to the shark's line. Any branch that holds both the rohu and the shark must also hold the land animals. Leaving them out makes 'fish' a group by way of life, not a whole branch.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of a clade: one ancestor with all the descendants.

worksheets.title: When genes disagree, and what the clock cannot tell (challenge)

items.p: Chimpanzees are our closest relatives. Explain how one stretch of our DNA can still be closer to a gorilla's.
items.a: The ancestor population of all three had several versions of that stretch. The gorilla line split first, and soon after, the human and chimpanzee lines split. By chance the human line kept the same old version as the gorilla line, and the chimpanzee line kept a different one.
items.why: A strong answer says that the old population had variety, and that the two splits came close together, so chance decided which line kept which version.

items.p: Different genes give different trees for three species. What do scientists report as the species tree?
opts: The tree most of the DNA supports
The tree from the longest gene
items.why: Each stretch of DNA has a history of its own. The species tree is the one that the large majority of stretches agree on. Scientists also report how many disagree, because that shows how quickly the splits followed each other.

items.p: Two scientists argue about the first fork in the tree of the animals.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives the evidence. For comb jellies first: the old arrangement of genes on their chromosomes. For sponges first: comb jelly DNA changes fast and may be misplaced, and a sponge has the simpler body. It also says what would settle it, such as more species or a new kind of evidence.
items.why: This question is not settled. A simple body proves little, because bodies can lose parts. A fast-changing branch is a known source of error. Both points are fair.

views.says: Sponges have no nerves or muscles. The simplest animal branched first.
Comb jellies kept an old gene arrangement that all other animals lost.

items.ask: Which scientist do you find more convincing? Give your reason. What new evidence could settle it?

items.p: True or false: if a clock date and the oldest fossil disagree, one of them must be useless.
items.why: False. The fossil gives the latest date by which a group existed. The clock gives a range for when the line split. A clock date older than the first fossil is expected, because the earliest members rarely leave fossils.

items.p: Two notebooks say '60' and one says '6'. One '60' was copied from the other. Why is this not two against one?
items.a: The copy only repeats what its source said. So the two notebooks give one piece of evidence, not two. It is one against one, and another notebook from a separate line of copying is needed to decide.
items.why: Evidence counts as separate only when it comes by separate routes. Scientists apply the same care to genes that are inherited together.

items.p: Rats collect DNA changes faster each year than elephants do. What is one likely reason?
opts: Rat generations are short, so DNA is copied more often
items.why: Many mutations happen when DNA is copied for the next generation. A rat can be a parent within months, and an elephant takes more than ten years. So a century holds far more rat generations. Scientists think other causes add to this too.

items.p: Sketch the fast strip and the slow strip as two lines over 48 rounds. Label where the fast line flattens.
items.a: The fast line climbs steeply and then bends flat near 12 squares. The slow line climbs gently and is still rising at round 48. The label points to the bend in the fast line.
items.why: The bend is where hidden changes take over. After it, the fast strip can no longer separate one long time from another.
items.art: Blank chart axes labelled 'Rounds' along the bottom, from 0 to 48, and 'Coloured squares' up the side, from 0 to 12.

items.p: One radioactive atom breaks down by ____, yet a huge number break down at a steady rate.
items.why: Nobody can say when one atom will break down. In a rock there are so many atoms that the fraction breaking down each year is steady. That is why rocks, like DNA, can be used as clocks.

items.p: Match each clock to what it counts.
items.why: Every clock counts some change that happens at a known average rate. The first three count chance events, and need large numbers to be steady.
pairs: One ring for each year of growth

items.p: Order these splits from the narrowest date range to the widest.
items.why: The older the split, the more hidden changes there are and the fewer fossils to set the rate. The ranges are about half a million years, 4 million, 150 million and 450 million.

items.p: There is no fossil for a certain split. Suggest two other ways to check a clock date for it.
items.a: Use a date from the Earth, such as when an island or a continent broke away. Or date the split again with different genes, or with a rate set from a different fossil, and see whether the answers agree.
items.why: A strong answer looks for a second route to the same date. A result reached by two separate routes can be trusted more.

items.p: Tamil and Malayalam share many old words. What does a family tree of languages say about this?
opts: Both descend from one earlier language
Each borrowed every word from the other
All languages have the same words
items.why: Languages are passed on by copying, with small changes kept. Two languages that share many old words, changed in regular ways, split from one parent language. The reasoning is the same as for shared changes in DNA.

items.p: True or false: a tree built from a single gene always matches the tree of the species.
items.why: False. A single stretch of DNA can have a history that differs from the species' history, most often when two splits came close together. That is why many genes are used.

items.p: Label three points on a time line: today, India and the Seychelles break apart, the two frog families split.
a: India and the Seychelles break apart: about 65 million years ago
The purple frog's family and the Seychelles frogs split: about 131 million years ago, further left
items.why: The frog split is about twice as far back as the break-up of the land. So the two families were already separate when the land divided.
items.art: A horizontal time line from 150 million years ago at the left to today at the right, with three blank label lines.

items.p: Two living species differ in 12 squares. Each line changes 0.3 squares a round. How many rounds since they split?
items.why: Both lines have been changing since the split, so the differences grow at 0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6 squares a round. 12 ÷ 0.6 = 20. Choosing 40 means dividing by 0.3, which forgets that two lines are changing.

items.p: Three of these are passed on by copying, with small changes kept. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: DNA, books copied by hand and languages are each copied from an earlier version, so each has a family tree. A pebble is shaped by water and is not a copy of an earlier pebble.

quiz.p: On a family tree, how do you find out how closely two tips are related?
opts: Trace back to the fork where their lines meet
See how near each other they are drawn
Check which is nearer the top
quiz.why: The fork where two lines meet is their last shared ancestor. The more recent that fork, the closer the relatives. How near two tips are drawn means nothing, because any fork can be flipped.

quiz.p: A tree is drawn with a fish at the left and a human at the right. What does that order show?
opts: Nothing: the order of the tips has no meaning
Fish are less evolved than humans
Fish are the ancestors of humans
quiz.why: The same tree can be drawn with the tips in many orders. Every living tip has been evolving for the same length of time. Choosing 'less evolved' reads the tree as a ladder, which a tree is not.

quiz.p: A bat and a crow both have wings. Why is that weak evidence that they are close relatives?
opts: Wings evolved separately in each, and are built differently
Wings are too small to study
quiz.why: A bat's wing is skin over long finger bones, and a crow's is feathers on an arm. The two evolved separately, for the same job. A lookalike feature tells you how animals live, not who their ancestors were.

quiz.p: Which feature best shows that a dolphin is closer to a cow than to a shark?
opts: The mother feeds her young on milk
The dolphin lives in the sea
The dolphin has a smooth shape
quiz.why: Milk is a new feature that appeared once, in the first mammals, so sharing it marks a shared ancestor. All three have a backbone, so it cannot separate them. The smooth shape is a lookalike shared with the shark.

quiz.p: Scientists first try the tree that needs the fewest changes. What counts as a change?
opts: A feature appearing or being lost
An animal moving to a new place
quiz.why: Each change is an event in a family line: a feature appears, or is lost. A tree that makes milk or lungs appear twice needs more such events, so it is less likely.

quiz.p: Why can copying mistakes in DNA be used as a clock?
opts: Over long times they add up at a steady average rate
Each mistake happens on a fixed date
Mistakes happen only once a year
quiz.why: Each mistake is chance, but a large number of chance events has a steady average. So the count of differences grows roughly in step with time. No cell counts years, and no mistake has a fixed date.

quiz.p: True or false: a scientist can predict which DNA letter will change next.
quiz.why: False. Each mutation is a chance event, like one roll of a die. Only the average rate over very many letters and many generations can be measured.

quiz.p: What is a dated fossil used for in a molecular clock?
opts: To set the rate of the clock
To replace the counting of differences
To decide which genes to read
quiz.why: The fossil gives a known date for one split. Dividing the DNA differences for that split by the date gives the rate. Almost no fossil has DNA left, so the DNA comes from living relatives.

quiz.p: A study dates a split to '131 million years ago, between 93 and 177'. What does the range tell you?
opts: How far from 131 the true date might be
That the scientists disagree with each other
quiz.why: The count of chance changes wobbles, and the rate is an estimate. The range shows the dates that fit the evidence. A study that gave no range would be hiding its uncertainty.

quiz.p: Which pair are each other's closest living relatives?
quiz.why: DNA, jumping genes and fossil ankle bones all place whales beside hippos. The other three pairs only look alike, because they swim or fly in the same way.

quiz.p: Fossil whales with legs had a double-pulley ankle bone. What did that show?
opts: Whales belong with hippos, cattle and deer
quiz.why: Only the even-toed hoofed mammals have that ankle. Finding it in early whales agreed with what DNA had already shown. An odd bone shape with no link to diet or swimming is unlikely to be a lookalike.

quiz.p: You want to date a split from 500 million years ago. Which gene do you choose?
opts: Any gene, since all change alike
quiz.why: Over 500 million years a fast gene fills up with hidden changes, and the count stops growing. A slow gene is still collecting changes steadily. Fast genes suit recent splits.

quiz.p: Why do scientists build a species tree from thousands of genes and not one?
opts: A single gene can have a different history
One gene is too short to read
It makes the tree look bigger
quiz.why: When two splits come close together, chance can leave one gene with a tree that differs from the species tree. With thousands of genes, the tree that most agree on stands out.

applications: Doctors and health workers build the family tree of a virus from samples taken in different places. The tree shows where an outbreak started and how it is spreading.
Scientists who protect wildlife use DNA trees to find out whether two populations are one species or two. The purple frog of the Western Ghats was recognised as a family of their own in this way.
Forest officers test seized ivory, skins and timber. The DNA shows which species, and sometimes which forest, the material came from.
Plant breeders look for the wild relatives of crops such as rice, brinjal and tomato. A close wild cousin may carry genes for resisting a disease.
Food inspectors read a short stretch of DNA to check that fish sold under one name is not a cheaper species.
People who study old books and palm-leaf manuscripts group the copies by shared mistakes, to work out what the first version said.
Scientists who study languages build family trees of words, to learn how peoples moved and met long ago.
