open_questions.q: Which animals branched off first: sponges or comb jellies?
open_questions.why_open: DNA letters have given both answers, depending on the method. A 2023 study of whole chromosomes points to comb jellies, and not every scientist is convinced yet.

open_questions.q: How long before the first animal fossils did animals really begin?
open_questions.why_open: Molecular clocks put the first animals well before the oldest clear fossils. The earliest animals were probably tiny and soft, and may have left nothing in the rocks to check the clock against.

open_questions.q: Why does the molecular clock run at different speeds in different family lines?
open_questions.why_open: Short generations explain part of it. Body temperature, body size and how well cells repair DNA may matter too. Nobody can yet predict a line's rate from how the animal lives.

open_questions.q: Is the deepest part of the tree of life a tree at all?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria and archaea pass genes sideways to unrelated cells. Some scientists think the base of the tree is better drawn as a net, and they disagree about how much of a tree is left.

open_questions.q: How many branches of life have never been seen by anyone?
open_questions.why_open: Most microbes cannot yet be grown in a laboratory. They are known only from scraps of DNA in soil and sea water, and new large branches are still being found.

maths.problem: In the Dice Clock Test, strips A, B and C had 3, 7 and 11 coloured squares after 10, 20 and 40 rounds. What is the rate of this clock, in coloured squares for each round?
maths.explain: Add the squares: 3 + 7 + 11 = 21. Add the rounds: 10 + 20 + 40 = 70. Divide: 21 ÷ 70 = 0.3. So on average, three squares change in every ten rounds.
maths.context: This is about the Dice Clock Test. There a strip of 30 squares stands for a gene, and a square is coloured when a roll of 5 or 6 changes it. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a count by a time gives a rate. Once you know the rate, a count of changes can be turned back into a time.

maths.problem: The Mystery strip has 9 coloured squares, and your clock's rate is 0.3 squares in each round. Estimate the rounds. The secret number was 34. By what fraction of 34 were you off?
maths.answer: The estimate is 30 rounds. It is off by 4 rounds, which is 2 parts in 17, or about 12 per cent.
maths.explain: 9 ÷ 0.3 = 30 rounds. 34 − 30 = 4. As a fraction of the true number, 4 ÷ 34 = 2 ÷ 17, which is about 0.12, or 12 per cent. An answer within 12 per cent is good for a clock made of chance.
maths.context: This is about the last part of the Dice Clock Test. There you use your clock's rate to work out how many rounds a secret strip was rolled for. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Saying how far off an estimate is, as a fraction of the true value, tells you how much to trust the clock next time.

maths.problem: Strip C was rolled for 4 times as many rounds as strip A. Strip A had 3 coloured squares, so you might expect 12 on C. It had 11, and it also had 2 dots. Explain the 11.
maths.answer: There were 13 changes on strip C, but 2 of them landed on squares that were already coloured. 13 − 2 = 11.
maths.explain: A dot marks a second change on one square. So the real number of changes was 11 + 2 = 13, a little more than the 12 expected. Only 11 can be seen. The longer a strip is rolled, the more changes hide like this.
maths.context: This is about the Dice Clock Test. There a square that is hit a second time gets a dot, because the second change cannot be seen by comparing strips. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Checking a result against what you expected, and accounting for the gap, is how scientists found that old splits look younger than they are.

maths.problem: Two kinds of bird differ in 2 DNA letters in every 100. Fossils show their lines split 10 million years ago. Two other birds differ in 5 letters in every 100. If the rate is the same, when did the second pair split?
maths.explain: 2 letters in 100 took 10 million years, so 1 letter in 100 takes 5 million years. 5 letters in 100 take 5 × 5 = 25 million years. These numbers are made up, to show the method.
maths.context: This uses the method of the Dice Clock Test on a made-up case with DNA. A known split sets the rate, and the rate dates another split.
maths.why_maths: This is proportion: if differences grow in step with time, a known pair gives the time for any other pair.

maths.problem: In Fewest Changes, Tree 1 costs 1 change for each of 6 features and 2 changes for each of 2 features. Tree 2 costs 2 changes for each of 6 features and 1 for each of 2. How many more changes does Tree 2 need?
maths.explain: Tree 1: 6 × 1 + 2 × 2 = 6 + 4 = 10. Tree 2: 6 × 2 + 2 × 1 = 12 + 2 = 14. 14 − 10 = 4. Tree 1, with the dolphin and the cow as sisters, is the first choice.
maths.context: This is about Fewest Changes. There you count how many times features must appear on three possible trees of a shark, a dolphin and a cow.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the cost of each tree turns 'which tree seems right' into a count that anyone can check.

maths.problem: In Fast Gene, Slow Gene, the fast strip had 4, 6, 9 and 11 coloured squares at rounds 6, 12, 24 and 48. The rounds doubled each time. Did the squares double? What pattern do you see, and why?
maths.answer: No. The squares rose by 2, then 3, then 2. The rounds added went up from 6 to 12 to 24, but the strip has only 12 squares and was filling up.
maths.explain: From round 6 to 12 the strip gained 2 squares in 6 rounds. From 12 to 24 it gained 3 squares in 12 rounds. From 24 to 48 it gained only 2 squares in 24 rounds. Each stretch of time added less for each round, because more and more hits landed on coloured squares. The count can never pass 12.
maths.context: This is about Fast Gene, Slow Gene. There a strip of 12 squares that changes on a roll of 3, 4, 5 or 6 is counted at four stops. These are made-up results.

maths.why_maths: Looking at how fast a count grows, and not only at the count, shows when a clock has stopped being useful.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that molecules can tell time? This card tells the true story of a clock that fossil experts refused to believe, and of the fossil idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1930s a fossil hunter named Edward Lewis found pieces of an ape's jaw in the Siwalik Hills of India. He named the ape Ramapithecus. In the 1960s several experts decided that the jaw was shaped like a human's. The rocks were many millions of years old. So they said the human line had split from the other apes at least 15 million years ago. In 1967 two scientists in California, Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson, tried a different kind of evidence. They compared a blood protein called albumin in humans, apes and monkeys. They reasoned that the protein changes at a steady rate, and they set the rate using a split that fossils had dated. Their answer was that humans and chimpanzees parted only about 5 million years ago. Most fossil experts rejected it. Then in 1982 David Pilbeam described a fossil face from Pakistan belonging to the same group as Ramapithecus. The face looked like an orangutan's. The old jaws had belonged to relatives of orangutans, and the molecules had been right.
how_we_found_out.who: Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson at the University of California, Berkeley. David Pilbeam, who first supported the old idea, described the fossil that overturned it.
how_we_found_out.when: 1967 for the protein clock, and 1982 for the fossil face.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the human line split from the other apes 15 million years ago or more, and that Ramapithecus was an early human ancestor. A protein clock, and then a better fossil, showed the split was far more recent.
how_we_found_out.art: Two scientists in a 1960s laboratory holding up test tubes, with a small drawing of a fossil jaw and a fossil face on the blackboard behind them.

roots.context: We have learned how family trees are built, and how chance changes in DNA can tell time. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Dice Clock Test, nobody could say which roll would bring the next change. Yet over seventy rolls the changes piled up at a steady rate, and you told time with them. Copying mistakes in DNA arrive by chance in the same way. So the differences between your DNA and a crow's are a rough count of years. They record how long your two family lines have been apart.
deep_truth.habit: We set chance against order, as if what happens by chance could never be relied on. We also treat a mistake as damage and nothing more. In this lesson, each change is a chance mistake, and a large number of them is steady enough to measure time with. The steadiness belongs to the large number, not to any single event.
deep_truth.evidence: Strips rolled for 10, 20 and 40 rounds ended with about 3, 6 and 11 coloured squares, though no single roll could be predicted. Human and chimpanzee DNA differ at about 1.2 places in every 100, and the clock built on such counts gave a date that later fossils fitted.

three.who_am_i: You are a cousin of every living being you will ever meet. The crow at the window is a cousin about 319 million years removed, and the banyan a much more distant one. Your cells carry the count.
three.what_is_life: Life is one family that has kept copying itself for about four billion years. No copy is perfect. The small mistakes are how life changes, and they are also how the family's history can be read.
three.what_is_this_world: The world keeps records of its own past without anyone writing them down. Changed letters in cells and changed atoms in rocks both hold a count of time, for anyone who learns to read it.

roots.thread: All living beings descend from one population of early cells. Each fork on the tree is a moment when one family line became two. Followed forward, the forks turn one kind of life into millions of kinds. Followed backward, any two living beings, however unlike, meet at a single ancestor. So the many kinds of life are one family seen at different distances, and the DNA in each cell still carries the measure of those distances.

teachings.teaching: The one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, does not turn away from anyone.
teachings.link: The Upanishad speaks of seeing, and gives no evidence of the kind a scientist uses. The tree of life gives a plain fact that sits beside it: every being you meet shares an ancestor with you, and the shared history is written in the cells of both.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 15.14 (the Mata Sutta), a discourse of the Buddha
teachings.teaching: A being who has not been your mother at one time in the past is not easy to find.
teachings.link: The Buddha was speaking of a long round of rebirths. He was not speaking of ancestry. Science reaches a nearby thought by another road: no living being can be found who is not your relative.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), chapter 4, closing paragraph
teachings.teaching: Darwin compares all life to a great tree. The green buds are the living species. The older branches are their ancestors, and the dead and broken branches lie buried in the Earth's crust as fossils.
teachings.link: Darwin drew the tree from bodies and fossils alone. He had no way to date the forks. A hundred years later the molecular clock began to do that.

science.text: All living beings on Earth share one ancestry, and any two of them meet at a common ancestor.
DNA differences can date the splits between family lines, with a range that widens for older splits.
Whether the deepest part of life's history is a tree or a net of branches that join.

other_view.who: The Jain tradition, and many working biologists
other_view.view: Jain teachers hold that every living being is a separate soul with no beginning, and that one soul never comes out of another. On this view two beings may share a bodily ancestor and still be two, for ever. Many biologists would add something plainer. Being related is a fact about ancestors. It tells you where two beings came from, and by itself it says nothing about whether they are one.

practice.title: Counting back with a cousin
practice.say: Sit by a window and find one living being outside: a crow, a tree, an ant. Look at them quietly. Breathe in, and think of your mother. Breathe out, and think of theirs. With each breath, go back one more generation on both sides. Somewhere far back, the two lines of mothers become one line. You do not need to reach it. Just notice that both lines are unbroken, and that they meet. Now look again at the one outside, and say the word 'cousin' quietly.
practice.kid: Sit by a window. Find a crow, a tree or an ant. Breathe in and think of your mother. Breathe out and think of theirs. Go back one generation with each breath. Far back, the two lines meet. Look again and say 'cousin'.

ask: Each roll was chance, yet the count kept time. Where does the steadiness come from?
A shared copying mistake can show that two notebooks, or two species, are family. Is a mistake always a bad thing?
The banyan tree is your relative. What, if anything, do you owe a relative so distant?
If you and a crow meet at one ancestor, are you two things or one thing that divided?

playtest: Every part was reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home, so treat the times as a starting point. The Dice Clock Test (the main investigation) needs one die, paper, scissors and a tumbler. It was run 20,000 times on a computer with the same rules. Strip A (10 rounds) usually ends with 2 to 4 coloured squares, strip B (20 rounds) with 5 to 7, and strip C (40 rounds) with 9 to 12. The estimate for the Mystery strip lands within 10 rounds of the truth about three times in four, so one family in four will miss by more. That is a real result, and the last step uses it. A child working alone needs someone to roll the Mystery strip, or uses the ready-made one. Keep a tally of rounds, because a miscount spoils the clock. Fast Gene, Slow Gene was run on a computer in the same way. The fast strip is nearly full by round 24, and the slow strip usually has 5 to 7 squares at round 48. It needs 96 rolls, so take turns. Fewest Changes was counted by hand: the three trees cost 10, 14 and 16 changes. The Brinjal Family on a Ruler needs a grown-up with a knife and a sheet of paper at least 22 centimetres wide. Who Split First? and Tree Talk were played through on paper for one and two players. The Cousin Mobile needs patience to balance, and a grown-up for knots. Ten Neighbours on One Time Tree needs the internet on day 2, or the dates given in the step. Nothing in the core path needs a garden.
